claim: Key differences: Africa is separate from Eurasia; a large landmass in Southeast Asia pushes into Australia and consumes New Zealand; Iberia and Arabia are missing; Sri Lanka is huge and is called Pranay.
The Mediterranean equivalent is the Gramid Passage, which joins directly to the Indian Ocean. It has two moons.
The year has twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days for the solstices, equinoxes and new year, and the year begins in spring; the week has six days.
Time units (hours, minutes) match Earth's.
Monster surges: cyclical events (every ten years) when magic spikes and monsters pour out.
The series' major surge begins in Book 7, about five years overdue, which the books connect to a magical link to Earth that had been bleeding Pallimustus off. (Later: Book 4-7)
note: Surge "some five years overdue"; the link connection is from the notes (Books 4-7).

claim: Animals include heidels (horse-sized, scaled, two-headed and horned) in place of horses.
Greenstone is low-magic: "mid-iron" density, which Clive calls very low.
The wiki calls Vitesse much denser, and the place files give what the books say about Rimaros and others.
Earth is the same template with a more rigid dimensional membrane, which the World-Phoenix reinforced billions of years ago, so it has less ambient magic.
It names ranks by category, matched to the spirit-coin colour: category one is iron, two bronze, and a silver-ranker is category three; it grades events by category as well.
It says "luminous" for holy and "affinity gems" for quintessence.

A link made roughly five hundred years ago siphons magic from Pallimustus into Earth: an Earth outworlder who had joined the fake Purity's church returned home with magic Knowledge had bargained from the messengers.
The siphon delays Pallimustus's monster surges, and the delay makes the eventual breakthrough more dangerous.

In the early books the outcome for a combination is fixed and recorded by the Magic Society (see 03_Magic_and_Adventuring/Confluences.md for the cites); by Book 12 the fixed combinations "are starting to add variety".
A person cannot advance until all attributes have reached the next rank.

sec: 3.6 Quintessence, spirit coins and other magical materials
claim: Quintessence (called affinity gems on Earth) appears as gems of an essence's theme (for example Dark Quintessence Gems; crafting material) and is used in crafting.
Iron — Category 1 — Four essences absorbed. Digestion changes; can live on spirit coins; sense auras
Silver — Category 3 — Can fight through blows that would be lethal to a bronze-ranker; some abilities allow flight at silver; the usual ceiling for core-users
Gold — Category 4 — No need to breathe; centuries-long life

Facts that recur: people of a higher rank suppress those of lower rank ("tyranny of rank"); essence users age slower: bronze-rankers can live well past a hundred, silvers can double that, gold-rankers live for centuries, and it is rumoured that diamond-rankers cannot die of old age; ranking up involves a "purge" in which impurities are expelled (often messy) and the body changes; advancing without monster cores is slower but leaves greater potential.

Spirit coins exist in lesser, iron, bronze, silver, gold and diamond forms. 100 lesser coins make one iron coin; each higher rank is ten times the last, so a gold coin equals about 100,000 lesser coins.
Coins from Jason bear his face and the words "PRODUCT OF JASON / G'DAY, MATE!".
Lodging, food and travel vary by region: Greenstone has a loop terminal that opens onto a street of temples.
Only the wealthiest residents of Old City have magic-driven indoor plumbing.
Vitesse's cloud palace has lush plants growing out of its walls and columns.
Rimaros has islands floating in the sky.
Communication: the Magic Society's water link and the sky link communication tablets, whose inventor appears in (the Sky Link Company).
A recovery potion tasting of strawberry schnapps appears in, and crystal wash in.
Each nature (race) has exactly six inherent racial gifts that can evolve with a blessing from a great astral being.
Celestines: metallic hair and eyes, skin from alabaster to dark; astral and holy affinity; not a natural race: two outworlders who have a child produce a celestine; excellent portal users.
Merfolk, goblins, valash (humans turned into them by transformation zones), lehenik (Nik's kind, from a word for "first").
Clive explains the cosmos as dumpling soup: worlds are dumplings in the soup, which is the astral, the source of all magic.
Interstice is the oldest and largest city-world, with administrators and no rulers, where great astral beings do business in physical reality.
The cosmos is kept in order by the Rules of Intrusion ("Laws of Intrusion" in), which govern entry into worlds that have not opened to the cosmic community. (Later: Book 2-4, 8, 11-12)
In Book 11 the throne is left empty as a neutral arbiter, and in Book 12 Jason learns it "could never be restored to what it was", with an echo of him imprinted on it. (Later: Book 11-12)

sec: 9.4 Astral kings, messengers and the Council of Kings (Level 2-3)
claim: Most astral kings began as messengers, a servant race grown on birthing trees, bound by a brand placed in the soul that enforces rank limits.
note: Messengers are born from birthing trees (B10 Ch4 L53-55); the brand and servitude at B11 Ch25 L51.

claim: Soul crests are magical tattoos printed on the soul, which appear on the body.
The Red Table: a blood cult with branches in remote areas.
The Storm Kingdom (Rimaros): city-of-islands in the Sea of Storms, ruled by a gold-rank Storm King; adventurer island Livaros, quiet Arnote, trade island Provo (the three public islands).
Boko: desert academic city north of Greenstone (destroyed in).

Other regions: Zartos (celestine underground city), Pranay (Sri Lanka-like; Jayapura), Kurdansk (Dreisil), the Dragon Lands (Antarctic analogue), Sadi Andali (lawless slave markets), Girlano (cartel-ruled), Segurado, Hornis, Kazlahk, Rakesh (first mentions: Zartos; Dreisil; Rakesh; Hornis; Girlano; Segurado; Sadi Andali; Kazlahk; Jayapura).
Astral spaces and zones: the City of Fallen Echoes, the desert astral space, Cardinas and the natural array, transformation zones.
note: Objective "Reach the centre of the City of Fallen Echoes".

claim: Books 10-11: the Cardinas expedition and the Death Pact; Undeath and the transformation zone; Gary's death; the aftermath of the sundered Cosmic Throne (Book 11, Ch64-65); Jason's interface becomes available to everyone with essences.

Books 12-13: Jason's prime avatar; Boko; the abolition of the System in slave-law regions; the return to Earth; vampire war; Knowledge's plan; at the end Jason walks to the standing stones at Ascension's Gate.
Team Biscuit: a familiar picked the team's name (the wiki credits Stash); Jason's biscuits are a running joke (Book 1, Ch78).
Dumpling soup (Clive's model): the cosmos is a bowl of dumpling soup.

The fundamental realm: the reality underneath physical reality, which Jason's Book 5 interface describes as "a space of combined physical and astral nature"; the World-Phoenix calls it what Jason calls node space.
note: Entering "a space of combined physical and astral nature, the Fundamental Realm" (Book 5 interface text).

claim: Transformation zones are the source of reality cores (shows the supply cut off when the zones stop appearing).
note: Node space leaks dimensional energy, creating the zones; source of the reality cores.

claim: Only diamond-rankers may enter without invitation; gold-rankers such as Jota Withers are admitted only as menial workers.
note: Only diamond-rankers enter Interstice without invitation; gold-rankers like Jota only as menial workers.

claim: Jason's Book 8 lecture distinguishes a set state (authority put to a purpose, "clay turned into a bowl", as in his spirit domains) from a potential state (raw, like enriched uranium).
note: Authority in set and potential states (Jason's lecture).

claim: Clive teaches that authority is the highest order of magic: the magic gods use for miracles and GABs use to regulate the mechanics of the cosmos, such as birthing universes and governing the rules of life and death.

Intrinsic-mandate magic is high-order transcendent magic that shapes reality by decree; Gordon's orrery ritual is an example: Jason is told that Gordon can use intrinsic-mandate magic, which operates on the same scale as a great astral being.
note: Gordon's magic is intrinsic-mandate magic on the scale of a great astral being; Book 9 Ch96 L36, Ch97 L64 show it in use.

claim: Akashic Speech is the speech of the transcendent; Jason's avatar inherits it.

sec: 4. The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering (Level 3)
claim: (Raythe and Velius's account; Jason's briefing in.)

sec: 4. The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering (Level 3)
claim: Book 11: the Keeper, the All-Devouring Eye and the Word in the Silence "ever stood apart"; the Celestial Book and the Seeker of Songs were against the sundering from the start; the Reaper, Legion and the Whisper in Corners "have come around and will fight" (Raythe).

sec: 4. The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering (Level 3)
claim: The Sundered Throne still exists, even broken; Jason senses it as a thread that rivals the might of the great astral beings.
note: Even sundered, the thread rivalled the might of the great astral beings.

sec: 4. The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering (Level 3)
claim: Some avatars of doom remain attached to it; they belong to the All-Devouring Eye and were loaned to the Throne.

sec: 4. The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering (Level 3)
claim: Raythe tells Jason that "only the nameless" great astral beings will stand with the World-Phoenix against him.

sec: 4. The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering (Level 3)
claim: Velius explains that the nameless "govern the functions of the cosmos. Life, death, time, matter" and are "unbound from the strictures of their duties" by the removal of the Throne's oversight.

sec: 4. The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering (Level 3)
claim: After the restoration the cosmic law is "much more rigid": the Rules of Intrusion, which in Pallimustus mostly govern holy wars between faiths, also govern dimensional invasion.

The Keeper of Moments (or Sands) governs the flow of time between universes and polices attempts at time travel; Boris says that time travel is the worst of ideas on a cosmic scale and that the Keeper "comes down hard" on anyone who tries.
note: Boris: time travel is the worst of bad ideas; the Keeper comes down hard.

claim: Shade tells Jason that, for the Keeper, "the past is inviolate".
The deep astral has no time or space of its own.
note: Clive: the deep astral doesn't have time or space.

claim: The Builder's synchronisation of the timelines of Earth and Pallimustus is noted as something the Keeper may not have liked.
note: Boris: doubts the Builder synchronising the timelines made the Keeper happy.

claim: What they are: "what amounts to sentient miniature universes" (Dawn to Jason); they forge "their very souls into physical universes, creating domains where their power was unassailable and all-but-unlimited".
Prerequisites: "you're an astral king because you have an astral kingdom... because you possess an astral throne and an astral gate"; the "astral throne, astral gate and soul forge trifecta".
Jason's body is a gestalt of physical and spiritual (: a healer observes that he "was not a dual-entity comprised of body and soul, but a gestalt physical and spiritual being", like messengers).
Boris explains that back then there were no limits on rank, because rank limits are a function of the brand, which did not exist.
Most astral kings are messengers: Jason is told that "the vast majority of astral kings are messengers".
Jason's familiars hold the source end of that power, which shocks a healer: no silver-rank should possess it, and she realises Jason is a silver-rank astral king.
note: Healer: the other end of the Voices' power in his familiars; no silver-ranker should have it; a silver-rank astral king.

claim: Colin can awaken as a Voice of the Will after hibernation.
After the Astral Throne and Astral Gate appear, Jason's spirit realm becomes an astral kingdom.
He tells Arabelle that being an astral king puts him on a different path from anyone he cares about.

Nature: gestalt beings whose body and soul are one thing; Jason explains that because auras are projections of the soul, their gestalt nature gives them aura abilities that body-soul dual beings do not have.
note: Jason: auras are projections of the soul; gestalt nature gives messengers abilities.

claim: A messenger seen in Book 9 "looked like a celestine with alabaster skin and long hair of spun gold... His eyes were solid gold orbs".
Messengers can hide their wings, reduce their size and diminish their beauty, and have hidden on Earth for millennia.

Belief and the instinct to kneel: Book 10 has a chapter titled "The Instinct to Kneel" in which Hess confesses to feeling it; Dawn tells Jason that messengers are messengers of astral kings, whose message is "Kneel", and that astral kings rule through them rather than invading in person.
note: Dawn: messengers are messengers of astral kings; the message is "Kneel"; astral kings do not invade in person.

claim: Rank: the books confirm that rank limits are a function of the brand (Boris), that Fal Vin Garath is a silver-rank messenger master and Jes Fin Kaal a gold-rank Voice of the Will.
note: Fal Vin Garath silver master; Jes Fin Kaal gold Voice of the Will at B9 Ch96 L10.

claim: A silver seal on messengers is mentioned in Book 9 (Vesta Carmis Zell "felt one of her seals disappear", a silver-rank seal, when Jason frees Tera), and diamond messengers can begin to resist the brand.
Social order: servants races (Benella and others) are subject to messengers; masters may treat them as they please so long as it does not impinge on other messengers.
note: Fal Vin Garath is free to treat the servant races as he pleases so long as it does not impinge on other messengers' interests.

claim: Methods: Garth's isolation (duel) power, aura masks, the world-taker worm and other apocalypse beasts, and the natural array's changes that devolve intelligence.
Resurrection: does not work on messengers or anyone like them; their life is not just physical and is tenacious (Jason).
Birth: Jason says messengers are "budded, not born" and are "actually plants, which is kind of crazy".

Boris Ket Lundi tells Jason that he is Unorthodoxy and that his astral king's allies do not know; Book 12 confirms that Navise Den Rigal, a Voice of the Will, serves a minor astral king who is secretly one of the Unorthodoxy's rare astral kings, and that Boris was slipped into the service of Vesta Carmis Zell.
Tera Jun Casta is a branded messenger whose brand Jason removes (: it was the brand of her astral king master, Vesta Carmis Zell, and it traumatises her).

The Council of Kings is, in Book 10, "the closest thing the messengers had to central leadership"; a group of prime avatars, each belonging to a different member, watches the Builder's agents preparing to move a planet. Many astral kings stand outside it.

Jamis Fran Muskar is an astral king whose avatar attends the Book 10 scene; his avatar stands out because its wings have been completely absorbed into his body, and in Book 12 he angrily accuses messengers of defying "the explicit instructions of the Council of Kings".
note: Jamis's avatar is the only one whose wings are absorbed.

claim: In a scene with Vesta Carmis Zell he says that when a certain task is complete the price is paid and Zithis Carrow Vayel, the Builder, will have fulfilled his debt to them.
What it is: great astral beings are the most powerful entities in the cosmos, and "the nature of both themselves and their power was known as authority".
Authority is "the fundamental power of the cosmos", and everything in physical reality is underpinned by it to some degree.

Two states: set-state authority has been put to a purpose, which makes it fixed, defined and safe ("clay turned into a bowl"); potential-state authority is the unworked clay, "except the clay is actually enriched uranium".
Jason's domains: his spirit domains are made of set-state authority, which he calls "the treehouse that I'm allowed to play in".
His spirit realm is also an aspect of his authority.
He thinks that if his domains broke down into potential-state authority it would kill him.
Transformation zones: they are "areas of set-state authority breaking down into potential-state authority", the domes being the world sealing them like scabs.
It must be traded: Jason says authority "has to be traded" and the Builder agrees.
The great astral beings' dealings are "striking bargains and making pacts", and pacts are about trading authority.
It cannot be taken: when the diamond-ranked Shako touches the tablet holding Jason's authority he is thrown away with a sonic boom.
Jason says Shako could no more take it than "burn down the cosmos", and tells him "That isn't the kind of power you can just take".
Shako has none of his own: "It is not my place".

Holding it is dangerous to a mortal: the authority Jason holds feels like a cancer that would likely destroy him if he did not get rid of it soon, which he suspects is what burns through vessels so quickly.
Gods and great astral beings know at once when a mortal outside a spirit domain carries it.
Shown to the holder: it resonates with the great astral beings and gives Jason insight into how authority and the beings made of it work.
Overcoming another's will to interfere with their authority is extremely difficult but not impossible, which is why gods have to team up to punish one of their number, and so do great astral beings.
The Builder's is about forging reality and the World-Phoenix's about dimensional forces, so authority can be changed only so far.
Jason used authority taken from the Builder for the cloud flask and his astral throne, and authority taken from the World-Phoenix for his astral gate.
Mortals and authority: mortals use it through intrinsic-mandate magic, which Jason reaches through his familiar Gordon.
Who can hold it: Shako tells Dawn she is "on the cusp of claiming your own authority".
She says she is now a hierophant, no longer among the servants but "my own agent".
Jason's special case: he accepted a power the great astral beings gave him, meant to let him do what the World-Phoenix needed, with set-state authority only.
Inside a spirit domain: even gods cannot spy on Jason there, as if it were territory from which they are excluded.
Shade's authority: Shade makes use of "authority accumulated over tens of thousands of years" for his self-sanction.
He refuses to let Shako take it, offers it to the Builder in a trade, and gets the way into the fundamental realm opened once; the Builder takes the authority back.
The original Builder: the other great astral beings sanctioned him for the twin-universe experiment by taking his authority and giving it to a mortal.
Dawn says even hierophants are not told the secrets of the Builder's ascension and his predecessor's sanctioning, which are widely held to explain his erratic behaviour.

The new Builder's conditions: when the other beings gave him "the sanctioned authority of original Builder", they set conditions, including the power to revert his mind to the state it was in at sixteen, as a messenger.
The Builder-and-nameless problem is described by Raythe and Velius.
The Cosmic Throne resisted, and the sundering freed the World-Phoenix from the pressure to be turned back.
Jason is then "in a state of self-sanction" and "has accepted external sanction", and the familiar contract becomes permanent.
The Reaper warns "Sanctioning can so easily go wrong".
Hero's planned self-sanction: Gwydion says Hero has decided to sanction himself, something he has considered for longer than any of them has lived.

Purity: his instability was coming to a head about five hundred years ago and he was likely to sanction himself, "essentially retiring himself and being reborn", until Knowledge persuaded him to leave a divine relic instead.
Gordon works the intrinsic-mandate magic, Jason guides it with will, and he reforges the god's authority with ghost fire into a divine weapon, at risk of Undeath taking root in his soul.
"Sanction" is not the affliction. The holy affliction Sanction reduces healing and cannot be cleansed while Penance is on the target.

A character who knows the affliction thinks sanctioning is that; Jason says "what I'm talking about is a different kind of sanctioning. It's how entities like gods and great astral beings punish their own kind".
Sanctioning is not killing. "You can't kill an immortal, but you can sanction them, which means to change them in some way".
Sanctioning is not painting over. Jason guesses it might be "taking someone and slapping a new person over the top"; Dawn tells him to stop watching heist movies.
Authority can be ordered over. Shako tells Jason "Hand it over, Asano", but the tablet throws him away, and the Builder concedes that authority must be traded.
Book 8: Jason holds authority for the first time and trades it back.
Book 11: he learns to use another's authority against it, and Shade's self-sanction makes the familiar bond permanent.
Knowledge tells Jason that even as a great astral being he "will not have the authority to sanction a god. That is for other gods to do", and Jason answers that he said he would kill her.
Dawn, as a new transcendent, "can't be killed, only sanctioned".
What it was: "the power that regulated cosmic forces, keeping the great astral beings adherent to their respective purposes".

Transcendent entities have effectively infinite power, and authority is "the right for a transcendent being to employ their infinite power in a specific way", which keeps the cosmos in balance; the throne was "the ultimate authority".
A neutral arbiter: the throne must be left empty, "a neutral arbiter without will, only purpose", as it was before the sundering.
Raythe and Velius want someone who will claim the ultimate authority and then give it up without ever exercising it.

The rules it enforces: "The rules of the cosmos are enforced by something called the Cosmic Throne. It was damaged long ago, but the throne has been restored and the rules are more dangerous to bend, let alone break".
Knowledge says the rules "have been put back in place. By you, no less".

Gods are bound by it: gods are bound to their worlds and last only as long as the planet they are attached to; Knowledge's crossing to Earth was only possible through the circumstances of the Builder's twin universes, which "would never have happened while the Cosmic Throne was intact".

The Keeper of Moments opposed the sundering from the beginning and refused to participate, and the Keeper, the All-Devouring Eye and the Word in the Silence "have ever stood apart from the rest, even before the sundering".
The nameless: the original pacts did not include the nameless great astral beings, whom the named ones treated "as nobility sees servants".
Without the throne's oversight they are "unbound from the strictures of their duties" and are unhappy at its restoration, but will not hunt Jason.
Servants cannot do it: "No servant of the great astral beings can be used. The pacts prevent it", so Dawn and other minions cannot repair the throne.
The chosen candidate: the repair needs someone in one of a short subset of transcendental processes, including becoming an original, with a pre-existing connection to the Sundered Throne.
The great astral beings believe the All-Devouring Eye created Gordon specifically for this outcome.

The sundering and its cost: after the throne was sundered some regretted it and others "revelled in their newfound freedom", including the Builder, who had always been bound by strict rules and began to experiment.
The twin universes of Earth and Pallimustus were "a step too far", the sort of thing the throne had prevented, and the others sanctioned the Builder.

The pacts and why they failed: the old Builder was sanctioned and the new one brought into the pacts together with the nameless, but this addendum "was not an effective curb on the behaviour of these late additions".
The nameless cause many lesser problems that "fester in the dark", cascading "towards infinite anarchy".

The offer: Raythe and Velius ask Jason to repair the throne while he is transcending, and the Reaper speaks through Velius to say that many of those who took part in the sundering now think revisiting it would be prudent.
The risks: connecting to the throne exposes his soul to intrusion, and his soul becomes a liminal space that others can enter while he is connected.
The World-Phoenix, which prefers things as they are, will be his antagonist.
Restrictions released: after the sundering the Celestial Book locked off essence combinations, so that each had only one possible confluence; Jason's repair starts to unravel the restrictions.
The World-Phoenix: before the sundering the Boundary sanctioned itself into the World-Phoenix and the throne resisted, "a constant fight to not be turned back into what I was".
When the throne is restored it takes the World-Phoenix's current state as the new baseline, so the pressure ends.
"The throne is a weapon." It is meant to be empty; its danger is the ultimate authority, "a power that no one and nothing should have".
"Restoring it undoes the sundering." It cannot: "The throne could never be restored to what it was. Part of you was imprinted upon it".
"Jason will rule the cosmos." He is asked to leave it empty.
He mocks the idea in a threat to the Reaper that he will use the Cosmic Throne to give everyone in the universe ten free resurrections.
The throne is split as if cleaved by an axe, the gap filled with blue and orange light, and Gordon's orbs shine and sing.
The great astral beings gather in their own prime vessels, including Raythe and Helsveth.

Jason says he is not going to make a fundamental change to the cosmos "right?" and every person with essences or their potential sees "Don't Panic. Everything is going to be fine. Welcome to the System.".
Book 12, the aftermath: his mortal aspect barely endures the task and he falls off the throne.
The restoration set "a new status quo based on things as they were at the moment of restoration".
The strictures the beings placed on the cosmos after the sundering are now being released.

Book 13, the rules back in force: Knowledge notes that the rules are in place again and that Jason, even as a great astral being, will not have the authority to sanction a god, which only gods can do.
They manifest avatars, speak with Akashic Speech, give followers essences and awakening stones that they can take back, and work miracles.

sec: 2. What gods can and cannot do
claim: In Book 10 a goddess says she cannot see into the astral space Jason is holding prisoners in; in Book 8 a priest says his god cannot see inside a building hidden from the gods.

sec: 2. What gods can and cannot do
claim: Domains: gods cannot enter another's spirit domain ("higher rules for higher beings"); gods cannot reveal other gods' deceptions, being bound by rules of interplay.
note: Gods bound by rules; the god of disguises cannot be revealed even by Knowledge or Truth.

sec: 2. What gods can and cannot do
claim: Miracles: "if you want a miracle, you need one of my servants or a grand sacrifice" (a god to Jason).

sec: 2. What gods can and cannot do
claim: Death certification: the Church of Death certifies deaths; in Book 7 an official is shown a certification that Jason has died four times "so far", and in Book 10 Jason shows Hana Shavar the card.
note: Certification says died four times "so far".

sec: 2. What gods can and cannot do
claim: Essences and stones: gods bestow divine versions of regular essences and divine awakening stones.

sec: 2. What gods can and cannot do
claim: They return to the god: freed cult captives with divine essences are weaker because the power "was not consumed by the process but returned to their god", and ex-clergy stripped of divinely gifted essences suffer a "debilitating imbalance in the body and soul".

sec: 2. What gods can and cannot do
claim: When the Healer casts out priests who exploited their healing, Dominion offers to take them into his service.

Gods and churches the text names in the form "god of" or "Temple/Church of", by first mention: Knowledge, Roads and Journeys, Hero ("heroes"), Purity, Fertility, the Healer, Revels, Deceit, Death, Dominion, Trade, Undeath, Lust, War, Liberty, Destruction, Disguise, Pain, Chastity and Rivers.
Undeath, Destruction and Disguise "have only hidden strongholds that are constantly being hunted", and Undeath priests are "the most reviled people in our world".
In Book 1 Jason sees temples such as the Temple of Roads and the Temple of the Healer on the Divine Square.
note: Temple of Roads behind the larger Temple of Journeys; the Healer's temple is among the Divine Square's central temples (B1 Ch94 L3).

claim: The fan wiki records the 43 gods below with the chapter of first mention.
The wiki also lists minor "profession" gods: Architect, Farmer, Gardener, Grocer, Hygiene, Mason; and says evil or hidden gods such as Deceit, Destruction, Pain and Undeath are worshipped in secret.
God — First mentioned — In the book text

The Greenstone temple was corrupt and had to be corrected by divine intervention; Neil makes a stand in the temple in Book 1, where a priest tells those who stand against the church that they are no longer welcome.
After the revelations about Purity, "the church of the Healer has taken over from Purity in dealing with the star seeds"; a Healer priest, Carlos, specialises in soul damage from star seeds.

Hana Shavar, an elf and High Priestess of the Healer, is in charge of operations that use Jason's cloud palace as a base after the messenger attack (the city's priestess); during the attack she avoided Jason's bunker and sent her priests into Emir Bahadir's; Carlos Quilido is a Healer priest who joins the Cardinas expedition.

A believer says "Dominion issues the divine right to kings and nobles", but Dominion tells Jason "There is no divine right of kings. Mortals choose and I try to help them not make a complete mess of things".
His church is the most prominent outlier in keeping low-ranking essence users under its thumb, and he tells his new clergy "There is no service in my church... you will obey or suffer".
He tells Gary "That is where monarchs come from. I love them most of all. I'll be keeping an eye on you, Gareth Xandier", and a character says in Book 9 that he likes "the ones who refuse to kneel".

Book 10 states that the Order of Redeeming Light was created by Disguise, a god masquerading as Purity: its Flames of Redemption are an extreme modification of lesser vampirism, and the order was founded only after Disguise took on Purity's mantle (Arabelle and Carlos).
Jason tells Melody Jain that her god is "an illusion. A disguise".
In Book 8 Carlos Quilido tells Jason his theory that the gods may have sanctioned Purity long before, and that rules of interplay stopped them telling their clergy.

In Jason's Book 13 briefing, Purity, who embodies several contradictory meanings, was unstable about five hundred years ago and likely to sanction himself; Knowledge interfered; and a relic of Purity's divine power was left behind.
Purity's most zealous worshippers carry many purgation tools; the wiki's claim that the doctrine treats humans as the "pure" state is not used here.

In Book 1 Jason meets the goddess as a woman with colourful clothes and Mediterranean features, beautiful yet "detached and untouchable"; she knows everything anyone in her world knows, including Jason, so she knows "Mario Kart shortcuts".

In Book 13 Jason tells his allies that she has been preparing to invade Earth for half a millennium and used him as a key part of the plan; the briefing says she promised the messengers' leader a chance to invade Pallimustus and claim Purity's relic, and that around a third of the priests and priestesses of Knowledge are her spies.
When Gabrielle Pellin refuses to believe it, a cube leaves her chest into Knowledge's hand, Gabrielle seizes, and Travis catches her.
Jason answers Knowledge's claim that she will be "the one true God" of his world with "The next time we meet, Goddess, will be the day you die".
The goddess of death appears to Jason in the Cardinas death chamber as "a stocky, middle-aged woman with a colourful dress" with the warmth of "a matronly tavern keeper".

In return he gains the title Keeper of the Cycle: abilities that apply afflictions also apply ghost fire, mana drain degrades the animating force of undead, and allies in his aura are affected by ghost fire while he suppresses undead.

In Book 12 Gordon suggests asking Death to return the resurrection power Jason gave away, and Death does: "I will return what was taken, Jason Asano, now that it cannot be used for its original purpose", the reality material forming Jason's prime avatar.
note: Jason's Death bargain at L18; "Can't hurt to ask" at L22. Gordon's own suggestion not read.

claim: The god of heroes is "the only core deity not to have subordinate gods".
note: Hero is the only core deity without subordinate gods.

claim: Those who make the ultimate sacrifice are offered the Cup of Heroes (Gary drinks it,, and says "I'm only a demigod").
Almost a year later Gary is a haggard figure kept alive by Hero's power.
Gwydion tells Gary that Hero has decided to sanction himself, something he has considered for longer than anyone has been alive.
When Gary drinks it, his hammer, fire and iron essences become divine versions and his forge confluence is replaced by a Demigod essence, not a "Hero" essence.
Hana Shavar says that the Church of Undeath lies dormant for generations and strikes when its god has "saved up his chances to intervene", bringing "dark miracles".
Garth Larosse, a zemravore and priest of Undeath, leads the church's priests in Cardinas.
note: Garth is a zemravore; Undeath priest Garth Larosse at B10 Ch88 L58.

claim: Undeath is one of the gods with only hidden strongholds.
The Church of Knowledge funds the Magical Research Association.
note: Churches, especially Knowledge, contribute to the MRA.

claim: GABs cannot interact with physical reality directly; they recruit others to act for them (Clive on the Builder).
Mortal form: great astral beings enjoy mortal bodies.
A vessel can be possessed; Clive notes it is possible, if far from ethical.
note: Clive: a great astral being can occupy a human vessel, far from ethical.

claim: Diamond-rank vessels of the great astral beings can withstand the strain and keep their selves, unlike the disposable vessels the Builder uses; eventually the soul can no longer cope and the vessel passes on the role, with no lingering effects and a stronger soul as a result.
No fear of gods: Clive says a GAB is one of the few beings that need not fear a god's retribution, since the gods of Pallimustus cannot see into an astral space that is not part of their world.
Dawn tells Shako in Book 6 that by killing Jason he violated the compact between the Builder, the Reaper and the World-Phoenix.
note: Dawn: Shako violated the compact by killing Asano.

claim: The Builder — Construction, forging reality — Original Builder sanctioned; new Builder is the mortal messenger Zithis Carrow Vayel (sixteen-year-old diamond-ranker when recruited). Vessels have included Shako and Erigo Fin Desca (prime vessel after Shako was taken by the Sundered Throne).

The World-Phoenix — Dimensional integrity — Formerly the Boundary; it sanctioned itself into the World-Phoenix because it wanted to be more than its role, the Cosmic Throne resisted, and the Sundering freed it (the World-Phoenix's own account to Jason). Female in mortal form; prime vessel Helsveth. Dawn is a hierophant.

The Reaper — The finality of death — Its followers' order of assassins used the Way of the Reaper martial art; that the Reaper gave it to them is from the wiki and not confirmed. Shade is one of its shadows. Its vessel in Book 11 is the celestine Velius.
The Keeper of Moments (of Sands) — Time — Prime vessel Raythe; polices time travel; stood apart from and against the Sundering.

The All-Devouring Eye — Entropy, annihilation — Stands apart; the avatars of doom belong to it and were loaned to the Throne. A messenger says Jason "has grown in ways only the All-Devouring Eye anticipated"; Gordon comes from its realm.
The Celestial Book — Understanding the nature of magic — Against the Sundering; Clive venerates it.
Legion — "Administers the cosmic rules that govern life itself"; its realm abuts the All-Devouring Eye's — Came around.
Word in the Silence — (not detailed) — "Ever stood apart from the rest, even before the sundering", with the Keeper and the All-Devouring Eye.
Raythe tells Jason that only "the nameless" will stand with the World-Phoenix against him.

Velius explains that the nameless are "entities that govern the functions of the cosmos. Life, death, time, matter... the functionaries of all that is", "very happy with the removal of the Cosmic Throne's oversight" and "unbound from the strictures of their duties"; the original pacts did not include them.
In Book 12 Jason is told the nameless "are unhappy, as they would be with anything short of complete cosmic anarchy".

Book 8: Jason and Dawn reason that the original Builder was sanctioned, perhaps by "slapping a new person over the top", and Dawn says there are secrets about the Builder's ascension and his predecessor's sanctioning that even hierophants are not privy to.

Examples in the text: the Boundary sanctioned itself into the World-Phoenix; Shade sanctioned himself into a Shadow of the Hegemon; Hero decided to sanction himself; Purity was likely about to sanction himself when Knowledge interfered, and the wiki says he expended his authority on a single artefact.
note: Knowledge convinced Purity to leave a divine relic.

claim: Obsession: "obsessed with physical reality while, by its very nature, being unable to co-exist with it", it is building a world of its own in the deep astral from stolen astral spaces; because an astral being cannot interact with physical reality directly, it "recruits people to carve off the astral spaces connected to their world, then it steps in and claims them".

Methods: cults; star seeds, the means by which great astral beings "send their followers" power instead of essences and stones, which turn a heretic's remnant power into a means of exploding themselves and which are "transcendent-rank objects" not purged by an essence ability or simple ritual; cultists and captives "exploded into crystal stars"; constructs such as golems and clockwork animals; Clockwork Kings, gold-rank native creatures of the Builder's world, dragon-like and not monsters, whose cores make the cult's clockwork cores.

Book 8 settlement: the Fundamental Realm Authority Token enters Jason's inventory in Book 8, and his ability to access the fundamental realm is lost; he looted it from the destroyed artefacts, and Dawn tells him he will need to give it back.
The separate item the World-Phoenix crafted in Book 6 is for establishing the link.
She speaks of the Boundary in her own words in Book 11.
note: The World-Phoenix tells how the Boundary sanctioned itself into her.

claim: Relationship to Jason: sent Dawn; in the Rumble in the Jungle, the soul-space battleground where Jason's team stands against the nameless great astral beings.
note: Nameless asked after; "Rumble in the Jungle" explained by the Seeker of Songs.

claim: Prime vessel: Helsveth.
Dawn is the World-Phoenix's hierophant; Soramir tells Jason that the Hierophant is allowed to intervene in the world a single time.
What it is: "the closest thing the messengers had to central leadership", represented in Book 10 by a collection of prime avatars, each belonging to a different member.
Membership: it "ostensibly represents the strongest of the astral kings", with many others outside it, "even a few powerful eccentrics who have declined to be part of our little group".
The council does not know how many astral kings stand outside it.
Authority: "The Council of Kings may guide us, but you do not rule us".
Jamis says he is a member and that some consider him its leader, "although it has no such thing".
Tera Jun Casta calls him "the closest thing we have to a true, singular leader".
Not absolute: the council's power is not absolute, as what happened in Boko already shows, and controlling it is "a delicate affair".
Rivalry: "Every person here is an enemy to everyone else in this room, yet we work together regardless".
Large operations are coordinated by meetings of Voices of the Will, the commanders of each king's local forces.
Vesta Carmis Zell: she sits in the Book 10 meeting, where Jamis tells her she is the only astral king in the room not focused on the larger goal and not some "personal project".
In Book 9 she calls the council after Jason frees Tera.
By Book 13 she is "on the outside of the Council of Kings, particularly after her losses on Pallimustus".
Outside the council: at a Book 12 meeting of Voices of the Will, the Voices belonging to council members are absent.
The council has instructed the forces not to provoke Jason, and one Voice says none of their kings belong to the council.

Hypocrisy: Jamis says his people have a détente with the originals: "We avoid them, and those associated with them. They, in turn, do not interfere with us", and the arrangement keeps the messenger masses from seeing it.
A few rebel astral kings fit within the council's ideological framework, so long as they do not highlight it.
Private agents: Jamis has agents on Earth that the council cannot access.
The Builder's planet-move: prime avatars of council members watch the Builder's world engineers move a planet, and one of them wants to destroy Erigo Fin Desca as a traitor until Jamis stops him.

Jamis on Jason: he tells Vesta he does not fear the rise of another original and will not annihilate every potential threat, since "our species would spend their entire lives roaming the cosmos, smiting silver- and bronze-rankers".
Boko: Jamis rebukes messenger commanders for defying "the explicit instructions of the Council of Kings" and later meets Jason, saying he would offer him a seat on the council if he would take it.
Jamis's offer: empowered by the council, he offers the withdrawal of a significant number of occupying forces in return for Jason not campaigning against the messengers.
Jason points out that the territories are the ones now useless to their goals, and Jamis admits it.
The squeeze on Earth: the council saw no value in poking at the great astral beings and avoided Earth, which was central to the scandal that saw the original Builder sanctioned.
"The council commands all messengers." It does not, as Book 12 shows when kings and Voices defy it.
"The council is united." Its members are rivals who work together and fall out, as Vesta does.
Book 9: Vesta convenes the council over Jason.
Book 10: the council watches the Builder's task, with Jamis restraining Vesta.
Book 12: the council has told its forces not to provoke Jason, is defied at Boko, and Jamis meets Jason (Book 12, Ch35).
Book 13: Jamis reappears with a request and a threat, and the council's ignorance of the Unorthodoxy colony on Earth is part of what Jason trades on.
Each physical reality is a dumpling, and "the astral is the soup through which we are all the dumplings... floating".
The astral is also the source of all magic, "pure, unadulterated; the most fundamental building blocks of reality".
Why worlds differ: some worlds soak up a lot of the soup and others very little, which is why Pallimustus has essences, awakening stones, quintessence and monsters and Earth did not.
Astral spaces: "think of the soup kind of congealing around a dumpling", giving a magical dimension attached to a world.
Congealed magic can drift away, especially if someone pokes a hole in the world's side, and can touch another world to form a brief unstable link.
Physical substance cannot exist there, which is why Jason's body "ceased to exist" when he was pulled through it. Only his soul, being magical, survived.
It is a single flat plane with no sun or stars, containing only the city world of Interstice.
It is "both the oldest and largest metropolis in existence".
How the city looks: oceans with interlinked artificial islands charged by great waves, hollowed mountains, volcano foundry cities and intelligent species of every stripe in jungles of ziggurats.
It has no sun yet has days and no moon yet has tides, and some call it "the capital city of the cosmos".
When the great astral beings have business in a physical reality, this is the one they use.

Arrival: travellers arrive by dimensional teleportation in portal squares in the submarine bowels of the city, where local authorities note arrivals and make checks; portalling into just any region is frowned upon and magically obstructed.
Many consider it the capital of the astral, "at least the portion of it that we know".
Astral spaces are borderlands where physical and astral blend, and the dimensional vessels powerful individuals use are mobile astral spaces.
The wall: Jason says that beyond the wall he sees in his spirit realm is the deep astral, shown as metaphor.
Every monster surge weakens the dimensional wall between a universe and the deep astral.
Until the bridge is complete, anything that tries to travel it is dumped into the deep astral.
The All-Devouring Eye's region, where the speaker and Gordon come from, abuts Legion's, where "life and annihilation are neighbours".

Who lives where: Dawn says great astral beings are in charge of the cosmos and inhabit the deep astral, gods are like regional managers of universes, and astral kings are sentient miniature universes.
Interstice and Jason: once Jason reaches diamond rank, Shade can guide him to Interstice, and Haliastur will introduce him around.
Power from it: Jason's astral gate taps the deep astral, "the infinite plane of raw magic and dimensional forces".
Each universe has its own space and time and serves as a waypoint for astral geography.
Interstice's population: only diamond-rankers may enter without invitation, and gold-rankers only as menial workers.
Residents come from the wider cosmos or from polities that span dimensions, such as the Radiant Sovereignty and the Constel Empire.
The success rate of getting from the feeder programmes to a gold-rank posting in Interstice is infinitesimally small.
The deep astral is a place for diamond-rankers, astral entities and transcendents, and a gold-ranker needs a patron.
Jota thinks of universes as islands in an ocean.
Who has been there: Boris has been to Interstice, which Jason says is too much to explain right now.
Boris says the cult of the World-Phoenix finds people, "not unless you can get into Interstice".

Travel: the deep astral is not visible in the normal sense, but its raw magic interacts with the ship's protective bubble, sometimes as arcadian landscapes and sometimes as a void with bizarre objects drifting past.
Crossing the bridge means crossing "the scathing unreality of the deep astral".
Jason's astral kingdom has a private dock onto the deep astral, which once led to the Cosmic Throne.
Its inhabitants: the realm of the fully spiritual "has no ranks in power", only authority to act or its absence.
A transcendent like Dawn exists conceptually in the deep astral and has no real body.
Clive calls it "an infinite ocean of unadulterated power".
"Jason's body changed." Knowledge's account is that his body was changed, but Clive insists it simply stopped existing.
"Interstice has rulers." It has administrators only.
"The deep astral is somewhere you can travel to." It has no geography; distance is a metaphor and only becomes real where physical and astral meet.

What they cover: "The Rules of Intrusion have always been in place. On my world, they mostly apply to holy wars, where one faith invades the domain of another. But, as it turns out, they also govern dimensional invasion".
Jason describes them as a body of rules about "who can invade a world", including how one god can invade another's territory to conduct a holy war.
Closed worlds: there are rules about intruding on worlds that have not declared themselves open to the cosmic community.
Earth was opened to the wider cosmos, which let outside forces in.
Bending them: the Jakaar pirate fleet makes its living on rules that "could be nudged" and others "pushed".
The lower the rank, the less strenuous the rules, so a gold-rank crew can go places the admiral's main force cannot, and a thin pretence is enough to satisfy the rules for a low-to-mid magic world.
A pretext or an invitation: the pirates are told that, with an invitation from the locals, they can "stroll right in, free and clear of the rules".
The pirates' condition for being allowed on Earth is to remove Jason, and if they do not do so swiftly they will be in violation of the Rules.

Cut off: while the terms are unmet, the pirate crew is "cut off from the outside", and the admiral, through the rules of intrusion, can feel that Earth's universe "was still unavailable to him, even through gold-rank catspaws".
Cosmic law is stricter: "There has been flexibility in the rules, going back to before the birth of our worlds, but that has changed. Recently. Cosmic law is much more rigid now".
The throne's restoration put the rules back in place, and "contravening them is not easy".

Hosts and guests: an invitation, "either literally or metaphysically", means the guest is no longer an intruder, and the rights of host and guest carry metaphysical weight that sharply reduces the host's ability to harm them.
Earth has gods, and the faith behind them is real, so she has to conduct a holy war, take the world, and eradicate the temples of its closest thing to a resident deity.
Domains count as temples: Jason's domains "function like the divine ground held by gods", so Knowledge needs her army to conquer the world and then his temples before she can take her place.
Avatars and half-transcendents: half-transcendents use avatars "largely to avoid violating the rules of intrusion".

Outside influence: a speaker explains that some people have lived somewhere long enough for it to be home, "but if they bring too much outside influence, they become outsiders in the eyes of the Laws of Intrusion".

The pirates: the Jakaar fleet's gold-rank crew enters Earth on the locals' invitation and is bound to the terms of the deal; Natala tells Jota that the rules leave them cut off until they remove Asano.
Jota's reading: he suspects the cult of the World-Phoenix arranged for the pirates to be Jason's first impression.
Jason therefore built the Earth anchor on the outback site, so that his territories remain bastions that Knowledge cannot reach until she has seized everything else.

Messengers on Earth: Jason reads a messenger's threat as meaning that the Unorthodoxy's choice to hide on Earth means the laws of intrusion would not stop the Orthodoxy from attacking them, so either the Unorthodoxy leaves or the Orthodoxy is free to invade.
"Someone will arrest the intruders." Lenora asks if the space police will come and arrest them.
Rufus answers that the Cosmic Throne enforces the rules, and that he does not know the consequences of breaking them.
"A friendly bridge into Jason's domains would help." Jason's Yumi suggests it, but a bridge into his domains would count as an invitation and give Knowledge access.
Before the repair: the rules had flexibility.
Book 12: the restored throne makes them rigid, and the pirates are bound by their terms.
Book 13: Jason uses the rules in his plan for the bridge and the defence of Earth.

The announcement: on every world with magic, every person who has essences or the potential for them sees a screen saying "Don't Panic. Everything is going to be fine. Welcome to the System", in whatever medium the species uses to communicate.

Why: "The throne could never be restored to what it was. Part of you was imprinted upon it. An echo of you, spread across the cosmos", and "You made your interface available to everyone with essences or the potential to get them".
What it does by default: it lets people view their own information and nothing more, but species gift evolutions and essence abilities are expanding the base effects, as they did for Jason.
How it arrives: the System waits for a moment of safety before revealing itself to an individual.
Most deaths come from reactions to the System, not the System itself: religious furore, superstition, and mass killings to keep the new power from teaching oppressed people.
Where it runs: it imprints itself on devices such as mirage chamber projectors, and people love the integration.
Terms: the prime avatar's sheet uses "nature" instead of "race", and Shade suggests the term now has to cover the breadth of individuals the System serves.

The System Administrator gift: it gives access to all aspects of the system, with extras such as maps, voice and image chat, party and raid groups and assessing creatures and objects, which Jason can grant to others.
It represents his relation to the System, akin to a great astral being's, with most control sealed until he reaches full transcendence.
Limited control: Jason says he has limited ability to manipulate it, around his avatar and in his domains, and cannot "use it like it's my personal toy"; there are rules and they apply to him.
In Book 13 he still lacks full control of it and a lot is autonomic.
Jason's perception: the prime avatar quiets his perception of those connected to the System, "a cosmos worth of muted mumbles" that is sealed away so it does not destroy his mind.

Disbelief: Anna Tilden suggests the System might be some cosmic force reaching Earth that Jason is leveraging early access to, and Jason answers with a System Administrator window: "I'm being as open as I can, Anna".
Quick recognition: the System is "swiftly linked" to Jason by the organisations that had studied his abilities, and the Adventure Society sends Miles to find Clive.
The withdrawal: Jason sends letters to the powers holding Earth expatriates, saying the matter is not a negotiating position and that to have the power and do nothing is an abdication.

A System message says the Administrator will "shortly withdraw System access" in regions operating with slavery, indentured servitude or similar legal systems, with no System functions, alternate functionality for integrated abilities and diminished or failed rituals, for an indeterminate period.
The reaction: a mob gathers outside Jason's palace in Cyrion after the System goes dark.
The Queen of Estercost and others ask Vandrick to arbitrate "your withdrawal of the System".
The diamond-ranks' position: Vandrick tells them that the diamond-rank community holds that the System "is yours to administer".
Every new diamond-ranker gets one big world-changing action, and Jason's is using the System to push the abolition of slavery.
He is told to handle mortal affairs like a mortal and immortal affairs like an immortal.
The cost: a Cyrion house adventurer says Jason's ideals about slavery "mattered to no one until you took away the System", and warns him that he has made many enemies by taking it away.
A speaker for a trading house notes that the loss of the System was already an issue, though they can live without it.
"The System is a natural cosmic phenomenon." Anna's fear that it is "some cosmic force" is answered by Jason's window.
"Jason can pick who gets it." The withdrawal covers whole regions at once, and access is reviewed region by region on his return.
Book 11: the System appears across the cosmos when the throne is restored.
Book 12: it is linked to Jason within days and withdrawn from regions with slavery.

Book 13: a System alert reads "[System Administrator] has identified a dimensional infraction and initiated an intervention action. The Hegemon has arisen. Beware his wrath," and everyone old enough for essences sees it.
Jason says the system is part of him "like a spleen", and four teams are linked by his interface in a raid.
Knowledge refers to him as "The System" in his coming role as a great astral being.
"In time, the leaders of the enemy became the Council of Kings. We became the Unorthodoxy".
The orthodox view: messenger society teaches that the Unorthodoxy is a scant few in the hidden crevices of society. Boris says most of that is inaccurate.
Orthodox messengers hunt them diligently, and an orthodox commander worries that talk of a traitor astral king is the thinking that leads to the Unorthodoxy and a purge.
Numbers and hiding: "the Unorthodoxy is scattered and lacking in allies. We hide because we lack the strength to fight, and nothing ever changes".
They use different methods in each place so that losing one site does not expose them all.
Birthing planets: messengers are still allowed to find their own marks only on Unorthodoxy birthing planets.
Earth does not have enough magic for the birthing trees.
Astral kings of their own: Boris says the Unorthodoxy has astral kings, "slipping back into the general population" among too many to track.
One is the king of Navise Den Rigal, a Voice of the Will.
It is hidden from rank-and-file messengers and is "one of our key weapons".
He had a brand placed by one of their astral kings to deceive Vesta Carmis Zell, says he was never put through messenger indoctrination, and claims the Unorthodoxy founded the Cabal.
He spent millennia scouting hidden colonies.
Marek Nior Vargas: he hopes that Jason's freeing of messengers will turn "dead wood" into "raging inferno" and talks of suborning astral kings.
Jason supports the Unorthodoxy in principle but says Marek would turn his people into child soldiers and worries about "victory or death energy".
Marek's people subordinate themselves to Boris.
Erigo Fin Desca: formerly Unorthodoxy, he says he has moved on and that there is little point fighting an oppressor that can turn you into a mindless drone.
Navise Den Rigal: a Voice of the Will whose king is secretly Unorthodoxy, and who slips Boris into Vesta Carmis Zell's service.
Tera Jun Casta: freed by Jason, she lives with Boris and his Unorthodoxy messengers despite her views on them, and is angered by messengers who want to join.
Freed messengers: the messengers in the Cardinas zone are not ready for the Unorthodoxy, since Jason's aura contradicts what they were taught, and Boris's own silver-rankers are the difficulty.

Boris reveals himself: he tells Jason's team he is with the Unorthodoxy, that the Cabal was founded by his people, and that his astral king saw what Vesta's plans would do to Pallimustus' membrane and sent him.
The Earth colony: Boris scouted Earth as a site for hidden colonies, and the Council of Kings left the world alone because it was central to the scandal that got the original Builder sanctioned.
Jamis says he has agents there that the council cannot reach, and threatens to reveal the colony unless Jason trades.
Boris and the founder's familiar: Boris worked with the Network founder's familiar to betray the founder.
Refugees: Jason arranges for freed messengers to be sheltered, as there are large and extremely secret Unorthodoxy enclaves on Earth.
"The Unorthodoxy is a handful of malcontents." Boris says it is far larger than taught, and Jali says if messengers learned how many there are, society would fracture.
"The Unorthodoxy is a rebellion." Marek says it is far from one, since "you cannot rebel against those without whom you will die".
"The Unorthodoxy cares about Pallimustus." Jason says the Unorthodoxy doesn't care about this world, and Boris replies, "No, we care about you".
Book 9: Marek sees Jason's work as a way to show his people they can live without astral kings.
Book 10: Boris approaches Jason and Erigo is revealed to have left.
Book 11: Boris explains the Unorthodoxy's history and astral kings.
Book 12: a Voice who serves a secret Unorthodoxy king hides her allegiance.
Book 13: the Earth colony becomes a bargaining chip with the Council of Kings.
Domain: the Reaper is "very big on the finality of death. Some consider it the true god of death, as all our god of death governs is the passage of the soul into the astral".
Where there is no god of death to guide the soul into the astral, it drifts into the Reaper's grasp on its own.
The god and the Reaper work in balance: the Goddess of Death and the Reaper "each have their areas of authority and they work with an ebb and flow".
The Reaper's cult may not trespass on the local god's domain.
A priest tells Jason that the goddess knew "each time you had fallen and each time you had returned" the moment he entered her sphere, and has asked that he be more careful.
Certification: the Church of Death confirms that returned adventurers are who they claim, and its paperwork helps with registration.
Alignment with a cult: the Church of Death is "closely aligned" with a cult that works with it, doing public-facing things while the cult is the hidden hand.

Three guises: in Book 10 Death appears to Jason as "a stocky, middle-aged woman with a colourful dress" with the warmth of a matronly tavern keeper, instead of the stern-faced man who normally appears in that region.
To Miriam Vance he appears as a pale male elf in grey Yaresh clothing with a voice "cold and hollow as an empty tomb".
In Book 12 she is a woman with plain features, pale skin and a grey dress with a faded blue flower pattern.
She says a miracle needs one of her servants or a grand sacrifice, and she has no interest in the sacrifice of lives.
She declines his two resurrections as "not enough".
The miracle that follows burns the undead to ash with ghost fire.
The pact: Jason makes a pact with the Pallimustus goddess of death, enacted by her guiding his soul to change itself, with no access to it.
He gains power to diminish undeath energy, which makes his aura anathema to the priests of Undeath.
Death's ghost fire is the model for the weapon he forges.
A talk with Miriam: Death tells Miriam to stand, "You still command this battle", and explains how Disguise moved slowly to take over Purity.
Giving back: in Book 12 Death returns the resurrection power Jason had traded, saying holding it back would be "petty... unbecoming at our level" and thanking him for stymieing Undeath.
She says the gods will pass with their planet, "yet you will remain".
Limits: Death's remit "does not reach beyond this planet, which itself will have its time".

The hidden kind: Carlos explains that many gods fall into two camps: those with temples anywhere there are people, and "the gods whose priests dwell in the hidden places. Gods who you pray to not because of something you want, but something you want to avoid. Pain, Discord, Deceit".
Destruction is not on his list, but the Book 10 priests work in the tunnels and the temples are hidden; the wiki also counts Destruction among the hidden gods.
The priests under Yaresh: captured priests are found with a messenger communication orb in the tunnels of the natural array.

The voice of the god: when Amos Pensinata presses a captured priest, "a new aura shrouded the prisoners, unmistakable in its divinity", and Destruction's voice rumbles "like an avalanche": "The souls of my priests are mine to toy with, not yours".
Jason, as a nascent astral king, is unaffected by the god's will.

His reply to a threat: "You threaten the god of destruction with destruction? There is nothing you can do to me... Destroying my temples only fulfils their ultimate purpose... There are always those hungry for power to replace them... Those who hunger for power, not to dominate but to destroy". The priests explode.
His aim: Miriam says the god has taken an interest.
Jason suspects his goal is not the array blowing up but the tree: "he wants it to become some kind of apocalypse beast that devours every living thing on this planet".
Emir adds that Destruction "wasn't too fazed by us taking out his priests".
Allies: "The Church of Undeath is one of the few reliable allies the Church of Destruction has".
Undeath's priest Jeff has a grandmother who is a high priestess of Destruction.
The limits of the god: Jason argues that if Destruction had the power to wipe them all out, he would have done so instead of talking.
Death will not say what Destruction had planned, since it is another god's affair.
Outcome: the god of Destruction was hoping for a seeping wound in reality from the transformation zone.
Jason tells the Undeath priests to step back and take stock "who won and who lost".

The temple and the creed: a believer in the Divine Square calls it the temple of Dominion and says "Dominion issues the divine right to kings and nobles. It is he who determines who rules, and who serves".
First appearance: at Jory's clinic he comes to take the Healer's cast-out clergy, "young and handsome, but with a look of disdain and faint cruelty", with an aura like a wave of fire.
He tells those who join: "There is no service in my church... under me, you will obey or suffer. Or both, as I choose, because you will not enter my service. You will belong to me".
Jason and Gary: "I love that guy," Dominion says of Jason, because "the ones who won't kneel are always the most fun".

He tests Gary with his gaze, laughs when Gary stands, and says "That is where monarchs come from. I love them most of all. I'll be keeping an eye on you, Gareth Xandier". He asked after Jason by name.
Thanks in person: at the priest camp he comes with other gods in purple and gold robes with a simple golden crown, and tells Jason "You never disappoint".
Jason calls him a "work acquaintance", someone he would not take for after-work drinks.
His church: the church of Dominion is the most prominent outlier among churches in keeping low-ranking essence users under its thumb.
Oppression-friendly: on Jason's lawn, Jason asks if he has somewhere to oppress, and he replies "I don't oppress. I'm just oppression-friendly".
He compliments Jason's pagoda: "You're coming along nicely, Mr Asano".
Interest in Jason: a priest says he can see why Dominion is so interested in him, and Jason is warned that Dominion may have an agenda for him.
Absent priests: a character complains that she has never met a priest of Dominion, despite thinking power and control were the Church of Dominion's remit.
The sin essence: Jason's sin essence brought out the authoritarian tendencies that got Dominion's attention.
The goddess Liberty "likes to keep a wary eye on Dominion's favourites".
A voice in the meeting: Dominion interrupts a call with the Yaresh authorities, and Jason calls his offer "half-arsed power-plays".
A speaker notes that "the god of dominion—the god of deciding who gets to be king—showed up for a chat, and not for the first time".
Jason's view: "Dominion is still kind of a dick, though", and the power becomes who he is, "not good for anyone. Except the god of dominion, maybe".
Advice: after Jason handles a fanatic poorly, Dominion appears by the arm-shaped temple, saying "It's religion. Showmanship is part of the deal".
When Jason asks for guidance, he suggests giant banners with his face.
He tells Jason "There is no divine right of kings. Mortals choose and I try to help them not make a complete mess of things".
A gift from Dominion helps Jason contain his presence.
Not what people think: a character says Jason told her Dominion isn't what most people think, and that Dominion said Jason should let people find their own solutions to indenture.

His priests: Brian, a priest of Dominion, serves as Jason's ally in the Cyrion crisis, saying that his church does not venerate power but "the establishment of power over others. Rulership. The exercising of authority", and that slavery, a subordinate god's domain, is "a petty tyranny".
and Farrah describes the temples as covered "in murals of people... being fertile".
Priestesses: a priestess of Fertility is among those Humphrey's team meets.

Food in a surge: the Temple of Fertility keeps secure stations in outlying areas with infrastructure to grow large amounts of food quickly in a small space, critical to stopping fortress towns starving during a surge.
Jason leaves its main doors with his storage space loaded with supplies.
Children without a partner: the church can let people have a child without ever touching one another, growing the child in a jar, which is how most aristocrats do it.
A speaker says there are Gellers everywhere and that one would have to ask the Church of Fertility about that.

Mixed-race births: one person says the church allowed an elf and a human to have children and purged his father's "impurity" to produce him, and describes another birth made possible with the church's help.
Records: a church record-keeper finds how the church helped Melody Jain have a child, which her order's overseers never knew.
A messenger of the god: a priestess in the full robes of the Church of Fertility, with young acolytes, arrives at Jason's door saying "My god told me that Jason Asano was in here".
Feeding Yaresh: after the messenger attack the Fertility church supplies all the food for the refugees and its priestess runs Jason's relief building, which he turns into a multi-storey food court.

In vats: a character was "cracked out of the vat" by the church before he learned to walk, and a speaker says he might have to recruit a priest of Fertility and one of Knowledge for a complicated plan.
He is advised to prioritise meeting the church of Fertility.

Velius's cover: Velius, a prime vessel of the Reaper, works on Earth as a fertility doctor, in a role normally filled by the church of Fertility, knowing all its magic that does not need divine influence.
In only a few years the streets are teeming with them.

The brighthearts' leader says excluding the Church of Fertility from the main city is especially contentious, since "we were brought to the brink of extinction, and they are vital to rebuilding our population", and Jason offers to withdraw his dominion over parts of the city so the temples can be built.
The Healer's Hearth ritual: Neil asks whether a procedure is "the Healer's Hearth ritual", suggesting a ritual named for Hearth is used by the Church of the Healer.

Organising refugees: after Boko's destruction, Jason says "The priests of Hearth and of Refuge will be organising the people. Who wants to settle permanently, who wants to find a new home, and who wants to wait for the reconstruction of Boko".
The first contingent came from the churches of Hearth, Refuge and Dominion, and others joined as the work expanded, mostly for the logistics of a population in the tens of thousands.
The wiki lists Hearth and Refuge as gods first mentioned at the Boko refugee scene.
Name and rank: Jason notes "the god of heroes is called Hero. They really stick to that straightforwards naming convention".
Hero is "the only core deity not to have subordinate gods".
Appearance: a leonid larger than Gary's demigod form, with a divine aura.

The Cup of Heroes: when Gary goes out to die against the undead, Hero appears and tells him his choice, not his life, was the sacrifice: "You believed that you came here to die. People keep thinking that what the gods want in sacrifice is their lives, but that is not the case".
He conjures a goblet, a dewdrop falls into it, and Gary snatches it, saying "I know what it is".
Hero calls his choice the reason both are there.

What it does: Gary drinks, and the window says he has absorbed divine power belonging to the god of heroes, which will leave his soul unless he is isolated from the god's influence, and reforges his body into a gestalt.
His hammer, fire and iron essences become Divine versions at Gold 0 and his forge confluence is replaced by a Demigod essence.
The aftermath: Hero acts "like a proud but sad father".
Jason, learning of it, speaks in a flat voice, and Farrah warns him not to do anything crazy.

A gift to Jason: afterwards Hero tells Jason he can only push the limits of his influence a little, enough to give him a gift as the Healer did: a Genesis Command: Source, a transcendent orb with "the authority to link power".
Hero says "It is the best I can do" and is gone.
On Purity: Hero guesses Purity turned himself into an artefact because the continental war made Purity seem a dark god, and says that is why he himself is wary of changing his own nature.
How he sees himself: "I am the god of heroes. I, of all, understand that actions, not power, are what makes one worthy of respect. And all I do is kill heroes".

He wants to add "another miracle option. Something less powerful than the Cup of Heroes, with less of a price", by making the relics of heroes who drank the cup usable again, "if only for a short time", so that "the stories of heroes past live on in heroes of the future". Gary is one of the reasons.
Hero's church: Gwydion Remore is a priest of Hero.
The church has collected the relics of dead demigods for millennia.
Appearance: in the Divine Square a glorious light appears in front of a temple and the people fall to their knees.
In her temple she takes the form of a woman with colourful clothes and Mediterranean features, "beautiful, yet there was something detached and untouchable about her".
She says "I am Knowledge. Everything that is, or ever was known in this world".
Omniscience, limited: she knows what anyone in her world knows, including what Jason brought with him.
Jason says in a recording that deities are gender fluid, "heard from the goddess of knowledge herself", and jokes that she knows his Mario Kart shortcuts.
The church: acolytes of the church check Adventure Society assessments, "don't try to slip anything past them, because there isn't any point".
Gabrielle Pellin introduces herself as an acolyte.
Danielle Geller will send her scholarly relatives to the temple's library, as "the goddess always welcomes seekers of truth".
Gifts to Jason: a token the goddess claimed would send him home and books on dimensional transgression, which Clive annotates.
In the Vitesse temple she tells Sophie, "Now is not the time to pursue this goal".
Temples: the Rimaros temple is an important resource for magical researchers and has a symbiotic relationship with the Magic Society.
Jason's survival: Jason hopes it will not be a big deal that people knew he was alive because "Knowledge told people I was alive".
Armies: Knowledge's church has been mustering forces around the world, with a small holy army near Yaresh that waits to strike the Yaresh force from behind.
She answers, "I'm the goddess of knowledge, Jason, not of very confident guesses".
Funding: the Church of Knowledge is one of the churches that funds the Magic Research Association.
Armies of nations and other gods lacked her forewarning.
She promised the messengers' leader a chance to invade Pallimustus and claim Purity's relic, and spent centuries preparing Earth for invasion.
Jason says he was "exactly what she needed" and that she tried to recruit him.
Annexation: the Church of Knowledge annexes the island that anchors the bridge on the Pallimustus side, seizing Storm Kingdom territory.
Gabrielle: a priestess of Knowledge protests that she is not of Deception or Conquest, and a cube leaves her chest into the goddess's hand.
Confrontation: Knowledge tells Jason the time has come "to fulfil your destiny... and open the gateway that I might claim your world".
She says he cannot sanction her, since that is for other gods, and he answers that he will kill her.

The hidden gods: Carlos says many gods fall into two camps: those whose temples are anywhere there are people, and "the gods whose priests dwell in the hidden places. Gods who you pray to not because of something you want, but something you want to avoid. Pain, Discord, Deceit".
These are the "dark gods" who "will do very well" if the Purity deception becomes public, and Carlos does not like "the idea of my actions serving the God of Discord".

Pain, a god or a goddess: a soldier thinks of Pain as a god, but Kerr answers, "Where I come from, they know that Pain is a woman", and refers to "the Goddess of Pain's firstborn daughter". Gods are gender-fluid in the books.
A byword for fear: Trenchant says that against an affliction skirmisher he would "run like the God of Pain was chasing me".
Discord: it is called out as "in particular" the god the deception benefits.
The wiki's list names them as evil or hidden gods.
The church: Anisa Lasalle is a priestess of the God of Purity, and a priest of Purity in clean robes attends the Adventure Society inquiry team.
The temple has church militants who guard its interests.

Collusion with the Builder cult: when the church's involvement with the cult comes to light, a number of its key members vanish on "previously scheduled sabbaticals", including the archbishop Nicolas Hedron.
The people from the church are detained under the authority of the ecumenical council.
Hendren: the archbishop calls out, "You think afflictions can take down a priest of Purity?" in the fight.

A bargain with the Builder: Dawn says "the god Purity has struck a bargain with the Builder": Purity lays the groundwork and the Builder helps him cleanse the world of what he has come to see as unclean, taking the abundant astral spaces and leaving Purity to rebuild civilisation in his image.
Clergy of the Order say their "so-called God of Purity handed our world to a being that would taint our very souls".

Purification ability: converts of the Builder cult have a purifying ability that comes ultimately from the god, passed along a chain from the god to a purified clockwork king, a purified core, and the converted.
Carlos's theory: the priest of the Healer argues that Purity has been replaced by one of the deception gods, most likely Deceit or Disguise.

Disguise is "the lord of illusion, manipulating assumptions and walking unnoticed in plain sight", and "if the god of disguises chooses to take on a disguise, even Knowledge or Truth cannot reveal it".
The gods have rules governing how they relate.
The ecumenical council: it was convened by the churches to judge the church's behaviour, and found it had been operating well outside its dictates for some time.
The churches either haven't been told or aren't saying, and the diamond-rank community has been digging into it.

The Order of Redeeming Light: Carlos and Arabelle conclude that the Flames of Redemption are an extreme modification of lesser vampirism, and that part of it comes from Disguise, "the god who was pretending to be Purity", with the order founded within the church only after Disguise took on Purity's mantle.
The Flames instil an absolute faith in Purity as a safety mechanism against deprogramming.
Death on Disguise: Death confirms that Disguise moved slowly, shifting the clergy over generations towards the extreme aspects of Purity's remit, and rejected the priests who knew the original.
She says the gods were frustrated but could do nothing, since "the hidden gods operate differently".
The Order of Redeeming Light's seed was planted then, before Disguise.
The "fake god": a character refers to a deal made "with the fake god of Purity".
She hid it until about a quarter of a century ago, and she aided Disguise in masquerading as Purity in return for his help.
