Corruption in Greenstone: Neil Davone makes a stand in the Greenstone Temple of the Healer, saying "This isn't about serving the Healer", and is told he is no longer welcome in the church.

The god arrives: the Healer appears at Jory's clinic, tells his clergy that merely not being shunned from his temples is "mercy enough", and refuses to restore their essences: "For that, I shall give you no salve. But you may turn to another".
He says the power-seekers are of no use to him and hands them to Dominion, who takes those willing.

A blessing: he declares the clinic a sanctuary for healing, accepts that Jory's alchemy includes "togetherness jelly" ("I'm not going to begrudge people a little... togetherness"), and promises rituals of sanctification and a healer to staff it.
Those who repent: he answers a plea from a priest with "You blame others for your failings?", and gives a slight nod of assent to those who accept responsibility.

The church in practice: Neil reminds enemies he is "part of the church of the Healer", and Carlos introduces himself, "First and foremost... I am a priest of the Healer. Before anything else, I'm here to help you".
The church opposes forms of punishment such as necromancy techniques.

Attackers' banner: some of those who attacked the Order of the Reaper's fortress wore Healer robes, which Jason finds at odds with the picture of the church as intolerant, calling it "revisionist history".
Specialists: Carlos specialises in soul damage from star seeds.
The church takes over from Purity in handling them.
Research: Carlos and three assistants from the Church of the Healer live and work in Jason's astral space, and Carlos, Arabelle and Neil advise on the design of the hospital in Jason's palace.
Hana Shavar is High Priestess of the Church of the Healer in Yaresh.
Compensation: Neil says the Healer gave healing powers that can no longer resurrect the ability to heal "on a body-matrix level" to compensate for what Death took away.
A friendly older man: the god meets Arabelle as "a friendly older man, patiently listening", with no divine aura to crush her thinking.
He counsels her to walk beside Jason, not lead him, and she talks to him about Jason's patterns of recovery.
Hospital: the Healer priestess runs a hospital in Jason's palace.
Neil's choice: Neil says he did not join the Healer's church by accident but to help people.
Early notice: Gary says "Undeath is bad".
A character recalls a zombie plague with a Temple of Undeath at its heart, whose high priest was the local mayor.
"It's like their god has been saving up his chances to intervene in the world. Expect to see some dark miracles".
Garth and Jameela: Garth, a zemravore, leads the church's priests in Cardinas, and with Jameela commands the undead.
Garth's tactic: "The harder-fought the battle, the more we have to work with when it's done", and every battle that does not crush them makes the church stronger.
Claiming territory: Jason sees the god seeping into the ground and making it his domain, marked by purple light.
Death says "Undeath has been liberally spending his influence in this place".
Appearance: in Cardinas Undeath appears as a living man in simple black robes with empty sockets containing a crimson spark, and a deep voice "like gravel being dumped into a silo".

His manner: he accepts that Death and Hero's interventions at the critical moment need a response, tells Garth he will not punish him for following instructions, and complains that his priest Jeff's grandmother is a high priestess of Destruction: "When dealing with other gods, compromises must be made, even by me".
He says "we are forced into another compromise" over animating a vessel that will hold only a fraction of his power.
The avatar: he allows an avatar to be drawn into the transformation zone to aid his priests, and it fights Jason and loses.
It is "just power and the echo of intent", with no active will behind it, since the god's will is locked out.
Jason sanctions its authority and turns it into a divine weapon (see../Authority_and_Sanctioning.md).
Jason's reaction: his aura becomes anathema to the priests of Undeath.
A visit in Greenstone: the god leaves when told to by Jason, and when Jason calls him "Steve" the others whisper.
The text says "The god of Undeath's name is Undeath".
Hidden strongholds: he is among the gods who keep only hidden strongholds.
Jason's view: Jason calls Undeath "a complete prick" in a conversation about the gods, noting that some others have been kind to him.
Among those interested: it is one of the handful of great astral beings that take an interest in physical realities.
Its realm: "The realm of the All-Devouring Eye" is where Gordon comes from, and Colin comes from the border territory with Legion's realm.
No blessings: Legion and the All-Devouring Eye "didn't hand out blessings".

Region: it is "where I, and your friend Gordon, come from, and it abuts the realm of Legion, the great astral being whom administers the cosmic rules that govern life itself. Your sanguine horror comes from this place, where life and annihilation are neighbours".
A silent being: the Eye "is not one for communicating, even with other great astral beings", and the great astral beings believe it created Gordon for the throne repair.
"There is little point asking questions of the All-Devouring Eye".
Apart from the pacts: it stands apart with the Keeper and the Word in the Silence.
Its stance is "least active of us all", a vessel says, and its last intervention is long ago.

Avatars of doom: they "are the exclusive domain of the All-Devouring Eye"; it has never employed its reality assassins for any task, instead loaning them to the Sundered Throne, for reasons nobody knows.
The seed that grew: Jason is "a seed that the World-Phoenix planted, but he has grown in ways only the All-Devouring Eye anticipated".
Its vessel: an orb of leathery flesh, larger than a person, draped in a dark green cloak, whose front is an open mouth ringed with needle teeth and a single huge eye inside.
Its connection: a speaker suggests Gordon's potential comes from "the connection of his kind to the Sundered Throne or the All-Devouring Eye", but will not elaborate.
Veneration: "I venerate the Celestial Book," Clive says, describing a blessing that triggered a racial gift evolution, changing the human special-attack affinity to a spell affinity, like the elves.
It is "fairly common for those of us heavily involved in magical theory".
Not a god of books: Jason first asks if it is "the god of books, or something".
It is named among the great astral beings interested in physical realities.
Approachable: its stones are described as "a lot more approachable than the Reaper".

A word on proportionality: the World-Phoenix reminds the Builder, "The Celestial Book wanted me to remind you about proportionality... The ritualist is one of his", meaning Clive, and the book will not tolerate a gold-ranker sent to kill the boy out of spite.

A network: those who venerate the Celestial Book "maintain a loose network, with ties to the Magic Society and the Church of Knowledge", and its symbol is commonly recognised. A man on Jason's world venerates it.
The sundering and combinations: the Celestial Book and the Seeker of Songs "were both against the sundering from the start".
After the sundering the Celestial Book locked off essence combinations, so that each combination has only one confluence; the restrictions unravel as Jason repairs the throne.
A great working of authority for healing would also have involved the Celestial Book.
In the jungle: in a mortal body the Celestial Book "merrily plundered each new food cart", asks if the Reaper's joke was any good, and finds the battle "a petty squabble. It's kind of fun".
It is delighted at the surprise of the gathering, although it later gives Jason accusatory looks.
Its warning: it tells Jason that if he loses, his mind will be destroyed and he will be a new person with no memory.
Later it says "all of our judgements are compromised" by the vessels Jason gave them, and that the battle is done and he lost.
Domain: "Even the Keeper of Moments, the great astral being that governs time, cannot [affect the past]".
Policing time: it "comes down hard" on anyone who comes close to time travel, "in terms of bad ideas, even on a cosmic scale, time travel is the worst".
Names: a speaker confesses "a soft spot for the name 'Keeper of the Sands'. I like the hourglass imagery", and Jason says he once heard the master called "the Underclock".
Vessel: Lady Raythe is the prime vessel of the Keeper of Moments.
She says her master "opposed the sundering from the beginning and refused to participate in any of it", which gives her freedoms others lack.
The Keeper stands apart with the All-Devouring Eye and the Word in the Silence.
Interventions: Raythe's master took an interest in Jason, and its prime vessel killed Mah Go Schaat to protect him.
Velius warns that the Keeper and the All-Devouring Eye waging war in Jason's soul would be bad even if they were on his side.
Why the link was left: Clive reasons that the Builder's synchronising of two universes' timelines can't have pleased the Keeper.
Time is "a series of interconnected points" and "any given node... can only be directly changed by those within it".
She asks Jason not to attempt time travel or time looping, saying that section of the time pattern is too damaged to tell whether he would succeed or cause a cascading paradox.
She did not kill him earlier because eliminating the one who would repair the throne would be a massive disruption, and Dawn talked her out of it.
Raythe offers to find him when no one else can.
No blessings: Legion and the All-Devouring Eye are not known to hand out blessings.
Domain and realm: Legion "administers the cosmic rules that govern life itself", and its realm abuts the All-Devouring Eye's region, a place "where life and annihilation are neighbours".
A sanguine horror was summoned from a "nightmare realm where the Limitless Legion met the Final Domain".
Position on the sundering: Legion is among those who "have come around and will fight".
In a mortal body: "the man with the antlers".
It speaks in a "deep, rumbling voice" and objects to vessels that Jason provided: "There are rules". It looks impassive behind its beard.
Its view of the plan: it tells Jason that he could have given them far more advantages, and says "We do not get 'used in turn'".
Fighting beside him, it says "You are throwing away a chance we have waited eons for".
Against the World-Phoenix: it says Jason agreed to help and that "we exploited that to come here", and explains that it is easier to make an immoral choice when you are not doing so alone.
Position on the sundering: Raythe says the Celestial Book and the Seeker of Songs "were both against the sundering from the start".
Appearance: "the woman with blue eyes" among the great astral beings in mortal bodies.
Manner: it identifies a phrase as "a song from Asano's world: 'Rumble in the Jungle' by Fugees, featuring A Tribe Called Quest, Busta Rhymes and John Forté".
When the others complain at being used as a training tool it says "this man is hosting the largest gathering of great astral beings since the sundering, and he's using us as a training tool?".

Against the World-Phoenix: it calls hijacking Jason's soul while his willpower is diminished "unconscionable", and in the throne room, when the Reaper calls ceremonies pointless, says "I rather like them".

Obsession and method: "obsessed with physical reality while, by its very nature, being unable to co-exist with it", the Builder recruits people to carve off the astral spaces connected to their world, then steps in and claims them.
He gathers followers rather than crossing the World-Phoenix.
Tools: star seeds, tokens, cults, constructs and clockwork animals.
The three-way meeting: the Builder meets the Reaper and the World-Phoenix, grandly says "I will be worshipped by an entire universe... A god beyond gods", and is told that "we are the rules".
The Reaper's terms bar him from interfering with Jason's birth world or producing new star seeds, tokens or vessels.
In return the World-Phoenix will offer Jason a power at the cost of no further resurrections.
Observers: the Builder's observer constructs accompany a group at a test, and Shade reads this as the Builder testing them.
The compact: Dawn says Jason's killing by Shako violated the compact between the Builder, the Reaper and the World-Phoenix.
The Book 8 deal: the Builder, speaking at the table, says "Authority must be traded".

Jason trades the authority token for the opening of the fundamental realm and the Builder's withdrawal from the planet, and the Builder replies "Accepted. Deal struck" before the World-Phoenix can object.
His voice is "like the grinding of stone".
Vessels: Shako is the Builder's prime vessel until the Sundered Throne takes him.
It was "a step too far", and the other great astral beings took his power and authority and gave it to a mortal.
The second Builder: "His name is Zithis Carrow Vayel. He was a sixteen-year-old diamond-ranker when the great astral beings recruited him to replace the old Builder".
A new prime vessel: Erigo Fin Desca, a messenger heavily modified by the Builder, with silver wings and amber glass eyes, is the new prime vessel.
He leads the move of a planet with the world engineers.

The conditions: the Builder says that when he was ascended, "they took precautions to control me": they can revert his mind to the state it was in at sixteen, brash, impetuous and arrogant, though he keeps his memories.
He believes they intend to restore his predecessor and move his authority back.
He wants to be "the greatest of astral kings".
Why he fights: he fights to restore the throne because the great astral beings could only do this to him by being unbound from their purposes.
Jason calls him a worse person than Thadwick Mercer, whom the Builder used as a vessel.
A weak replacement: of the new Builder, Jason says "it turns out that he's... not great".
Domain: "The Reaper is very big on the finality of death. Some consider it the true god of death, as all our god of death governs is the passage of the soul into the astral".
Items and orders: the Way of the Reaper is a set of skill books, and the Order of the Reaper's teachings are collected in its legacy.
The Order of the Reaper used ancient knowledge of how to anchor such realms, "provided by the Reaper itself".
Reaper awakening stones give mostly aggressive utility and conjuration powers.
Speaking through Velius: when the Reaper takes over its vessel, the warm voice becomes "cold and bleak".
It tells the Builder that Jason "carried the World-Phoenix's token. Those pacts are older than you and I will not violate them".
The rules: "We are the rules. To deny them is to deny ourselves".
It arranges the compromise between the Builder and the World-Phoenix and makes its own concession, because it fears being made a farce if Jason is resurrected over and over.
Shade: "Of all my children, Shade has ever followed his own path", the Reaper says, with a brief fatherly smile.
A favour: Dawn says the Reaper offered to bring Farrah back, because it wanted to stop the World-Phoenix sending Jason's soul back and forth across the astral with tokens.
It was among the first to notice its former offshoot order moving again, but is hard to infiltrate.
The resurrection: Jason says "The Reaper resurrected her, not me. The World-Phoenix convinced him because she was worried I'd go nuts and let the whole planet die".
The throne: through Velius the Reaper says many of those who took part in the sundering now think revisiting it would be prudent, and later fights Jason in his soul as one of the opponents.
Its servant Velius is a fertility doctor on Earth in the aftermath.
A joke: Jason calls everyone to hear that the Reaper made a joke, and the Celestial Book asks whether it was any good.
A walk with the World-Phoenix: afterwards the Reaper and the World-Phoenix walk an empty road for two years.
The World-Phoenix accuses it of raising its vessels "like pets instead of using them like tools", and it answers that she got sad when her boy left home.
Sanctioning: when Shade sanctions himself, the Reaper warns that "Sanctioning can so easily go wrong".
Bending a rule: Jason says the Reaper decided to "bend his own rules, one last time, before the rules were locked in once more", allowing Gary to reincarnate near people who knew him.
Its children: Shade and Umber are the Reaper's children and brothers who drifted apart.
Position on the sundering: it is among those who "have come around and will fight".
Appearance: "the woman in lace", laced and veiled, "not a great astral being Jason had heard of" before.
Voice: "Her mouth did not move, her voice instead a susurrus of whispers all around them".

On forcing souls: it warns the World-Phoenix that there are lines even great astral beings should not cross, and asks "Will you become like the Builder, World-Phoenix? Forcing your way into unwilling souls".
It later asks why she would entice others to stand against her.

Apart from the pacts: Velius says of those who stood aside from the sundering, "They have ever stood apart from the rest, even before the sundering. The Keeper, the All-Devouring Eye, the Word in the Silence".
The mark on Jason: his first status screens carry a symbol of a fire bird, and an ability labelled "Authority of the World Phoenix".
Jason says the World-Phoenix gave him "a gift as his soul passed through the astral", and that he is an outworlder through "happenstance".
Its role: "the integrity of dimensions is mine. It is only with my permission that you can conduct your little game". The Builder will not cross it.
The meeting of three: the World-Phoenix attends in a celestine vessel with alabaster skin and ruby hair, "a teasing smile and an amused twinkle in her red, gemstone eyes".
She calls Jason "a pleasantly effective little seedling", and negotiates with the Reaper over terms that forbid the Builder from interfering with Jason's world.
How it acts: "The World-Phoenix does not like to act directly. It prefers to set things in motion that will ultimately achieve the end it desires".
Jason receives "the blessing of the World-Phoenix".
The cult: its head is the First Servant, the ultimate arbiter before the World-Phoenix itself.
Dawn says she cannot sneak past the World-Phoenix, and that it and she as its representative have always sought to sanction interference with the physical-astral boundary.
Avoiding confrontation: the World-Phoenix is "notoriously averse to direct confrontation".
It crafts a bridge for Jason as compensation, Dawn says, "a sliver of hope in his darkest hour".
A tool that fails: Dawn says the World-Phoenix "doesn't care about me or my wellbeing because it can't. What it can recognise is when a tool... is not functioning the way it should".
Speaking through Dawn: at the table in Book 8, the World-Phoenix speaks through Dawn, "a lot more sultry than I expected", and thanks Jason for reminding Dawn of her mortality.
It grins and the vessel's eyes return to normal.
Former servant: Dawn is no longer First Sister, and her successor is Helsveth.
Not a friend in the soul: Jason says the World-Phoenix "had to know what she was doing to me".
In Book 11 Raythe says it prefers the current state of affairs and will be his antagonist in the battle for the throne.
The battle: the World-Phoenix leads a horde of monsters in Jason's soul, asks him why he struggles, and says his will is in tatters in a matter-of-fact voice.
When the great astral beings are given mortal vessels, it realises "he is trying to infect us with mortal morality".
The Boundary: she explains that before the sundering she was the Boundary, who sanctioned herself because she wanted to be more than her role.
After: for two years the World-Phoenix and the Reaper walk an empty road together, with one pause when she says "I miss food".
When Jason arrives, she is surprised, and he talks about the Rumble in the Jungle.
The restored throne takes her current state as its baseline.
In Book 12 and 13: the cult of the World-Phoenix opens the universe to gold-rankers at Jason's request, and the World-Phoenix leaves Jason a message through Helsveth, who has fought him before.
In a magic-rich world it condenses into things: monsters, which are living and unstable; essences, quintessence and awakening stones, which are not alive and stay until used.
How many essences can a person have? Four, and the fourth is a confluence.
What are the ranks? Iron, bronze, silver, gold and diamond, with gods and great astral beings outside the ladder.
How long do ranked people live? Bronze well past a hundred, silver double that, gold for centuries.
Can a person refuse the confluence? Only clergy do, and nobody else should.
What does a core do? It speeds advancement and damages potential.
How long do monsters last? From a week or two for the lowest to a month at iron, longer above.
How common are surges? About every ten years, anywhere from eight to thirteen.
Level 1: Books 1 to 3 establish the basics above, and the Reaper trials and Builder astral space add growth items, familiars and divine stones.
Level 2: Book 4 moves to Earth, where magical ranks are named tiers that start at zero.
The Grid works as interconnected rituals built from the natural features of the world.
Book 5 and Book 6 bring monster waves and transformation zones.
Book 7 and Book 8 run a surge on Pallimustus.
Level 3: After Jason's second zone, magic on Earth "had risen" and essences and monsters appear directly. Confluences stop being fixed. Resurrection becomes harder. The System spreads from Jason.
That a pile of quintessence can stand in for an essence. Farrah calls it impossible.
The books treat that as a religious claim, with Rufus's answer that accountability is the wielder's.
That rank is the same as power. It is magical density.
[Wiki Reference Lists] (spoiler level 3): The wiki lists the essences below by rarity, with the abilities and users it records for each.
Belinda Callahan's Power Set (spoiler level 1): Belinda is the team's trickster and utility caster: Magic, Trap and Adept, producing the Charlatan confluence.
Clive Standish's Power Set (spoiler level 1): Clive is the team's battlemage and ritualist: Magic, Rune, Balance and the Karmic confluence.
Farrah Hurin's Power Set (spoiler level 2): Farrah is a volcano-themed battlemage and ritualist: Earth, Fire and Potent, which form the Volcano confluence.
Gary's Power Set (spoiler level 1): Gary is a leonid smith-warrior: hammer, fire, iron and the forge confluence.
Humphrey Geller's Power Set (spoiler level 1): Humphrey is the team's heavy hitter: "simple, reliable power".
Neil Davone's Power Set (spoiler level 1): Neil is the team's healer and shield-caster: Shield, Growth and Renewal, producing the Prosperity confluence (Jason's notebook).
The five abilities. An essence "imbues 1 awakened essence ability and 4 unawakened essence abilities".
The awakened one is a function of the essence and the person: Jason's dark essence gave Midnight Eyes at absorption, blood gave Blood Harvest, sin gave Punish and doom gave Inexorable Doom.
Special attack (melee, drain, wounding, blood): Leech Bite.
Spell (drain): Blood Harvest.
Special ability (dimension, teleport): Path of Shadows.
Aura (holy, unholy): Hegemony.
Conjuration (darkness, light, dimension): Cloak of Night.
Familiar (ritual, summon): Sanguine Horror.

Cost, cooldown, rank. An ability screen lists a cost in mana, stamina or both, in words (low, moderate, and so on), a cooldown (none, or a time such as forty seconds) and a current rank with a percentage: "Current rank: Iron 0 (00%)".
Mirage Step costs "low stamina and mana" with a forty-second cooldown.

Rank within an ability. Within a rank an ability also has a level and a percentage, so the same spell reads "Iron 0 (00%)" when first awakened and "Iron 1 (19%)" a few chapters later with a stronger effect.
An ability keeps one effect per rank, so its description lists an iron effect, a bronze effect, and so on, and the later effects add to the earlier ones (shows Cloak of Night).
Ranking an ability. An ability reaches its next rank as a separate event: "Ability [Midnight Eyes] (Dark) has reached Bronze 0 (00%)".
Several abilities reach Bronze 0 in the same stretch of Book 3: [Sanguine Horror], [Hegemony], [Path of Shadows] and [Blade of Doom].
An ability can be held back: "Ability [Cloak of Night] (Dark) cannot advance further until all attributes have reached silver rank".
Each essence bonds to one of them and raises it from normal to iron: "[Blood Essence] has bonded to your [Power] attribute", dark to Speed, sin to Recovery, and doom to Spirit.
"Master all blood essence abilities to increase your [Power] attribute".
Once an essence's abilities are all awakened, the linked attribute "will advance in conjunction with lowest-rank" ability of that essence.
Rank progress. Progress to the next rank counts essences complete: "Progress to bronze rank: 50% (4/4 essences complete)" and a smaller fraction for fewer completed essences.
All of a person's attributes must reach the new rank before an ability can go further. See Ranks_and_Advancement.md.

Knowing what an ability does. Ordinary essence users must feel their way into a power by instinct; "unlike other essence users, Jason had never been forced to fathom out his abilities by feel", because he has System messages.
The Magic Society keeps records of what abilities do at later ranks, and Clive urges Jason to look them up.

Cost versus effect. An ability may cost nothing, or may allow a higher spend for more effect: Punition at silver can be raised from a base cost to high, very high or extreme mana, which shortens its cooldown to twenty seconds, ten seconds or none.
Passive powers. Auras are passive and projected; Jason notes that an aura power common to the force confluence is able to move things physically, which none of his can do.
Racial gifts. Races have gifts that interact with abilities: humans' aptitude for special attacks over spells, Kylie's vision confluence letting her awaken a perception power from each essence.
Variable subtypes. A spell can have "variable subtypes, contingent on effect".
Abilities that outgrow their text. Jason notes that the wording of Cloak of Night has changed from earlier iterations and wonders whether his own perception shaped it.
Execute and retribution. Some abilities hit damaged targets harder (execute), such as Verdict, "deals transcendent damage. Scales with injury level of target".

Jason's twenty. Dark (Midnight Eyes, Cloak of Night, Path of Shadows, Hand of the Reaper, Shadow of the Hegemon), blood (Blood Harvest, Leech Bite, Feast of Blood, Sanguine Horror, Haemorrhage), sin (Punish, Feast of Absolution, Sin Eater, Hegemony, Castigate) and doom (Inexorable Doom, Punition, Blade of Doom, Verdict, Avatar of Doom).
Sophie. Mirage Step is the last of her five mystic abilities, and she awakened confluence abilities before her essence abilities, which Clive calls "quite unusual".
Clive. His Enact Ritual makes drawing and performing rituals more convenient.
Gary. His replaced abilities Craftsman's Gaze and Stoke the Forge become All-Seeing Eye and First Son of the Leonids when he takes divine essences.

Strong abilities are better. Farrah and Rufus both lay out a scale from individually strong abilities to abilities that "underwhelm in isolation, but used together become very dangerous", with affliction specialists at the second end. "Simple doesn't mean bad".
Combat power matters most. Gary: "just having a bunch of destructive combat powers makes you less useful to a team", and a few good utility powers help one get jobs.
An ability is its description. The description may not reveal all later effects, and costs for lower-rank effects are removed when abilities rank up.
Level 2: Abilities scale with rank into effects the earlier text hints at, like Path of Shadows from a single teleport to portals across regional, continental and global distances.
Jason's Interface gift gives the same display to others in his party.
Level 3: Jason's gold-rank sheet in Book 12 records twenty abilities at gold 3 to gold 5, with attributes at gold 3 and 4 and progress to diamond at 38 percent. See Jason_Power_Set_Reference.md.
What an adventurer does. Rufus: "The bulk of our job as adventurers is hunting them down before they reach that stage", meaning the aggressive end of a monster's life.
Farrah and Rufus both reject the idea that adventuring is "just going places and killing everyone you find".

Notices. A monster notice, "whether from a notice board or the Adventure Society directly, has three pieces of information, so long as that information is known. The name of the monster, or a description. The number of monsters, and the approximate location".
The jobs hall. The jobs hall is "an annex of the main administration building", "a moderate-sized room divided into rows by standing bulletin boards" with a desk where a clerk records contracts.

Contracts for areas near the city are in the hall; "those further afield were posted on each town or village's noticeboard", and every month the Society sends people to patrol those areas for a full month away, "not a popular task".
A director can change how notices are posted: Greenstone's new director stopped keeping a separate board for incentivised contracts.

Pay and bonuses. The Society pays iron spirit coins for an iron-rank monster contract, ten up to a hundred depending on number, travel and difficulty; bonuses can run "all the way up to an awakening stone, although such a reward was extremely rare".
The Society "was known to give out awakening stones for exceptional service, although rarely".
As a rule, "we don't give out awakening stones to people for killing monsters above their rank. It would just incentivise people getting themselves killed trying to jump ranks".
Badges and stars. A new member gets a badge, a circular iron medallion embossed with a sword and rod crossed over a shield, "one-star, iron rank".
The ranking system "has two parts": the first is the member's essence rank, and the second is stars, "not an assessment of your power, but your judgement".
Everyone begins at one star and the maximum is three.
One-star contracts "are pure monster hunts, with no complicated elements to deal with".
Two stars mean "at least some level of actual, unsupervised responsibility", investigating "potentially dangerous situations or unknown phenomena", and leading small expeditions of one-star members.
Three stars means "they trust you to handle yourself when things get political", and three-star members are "expected to anticipate and manage consequences at a higher level".
"You can expect to drop a star rank each time you increase a tier in power".
The badge confers prestige, not authority: "any actual authority comes from the contract you are carrying out".
Society officials are outside the rating system.
The badge does not track the wearer if their aura resists tracking.

Teams. "Rick's team had an archetypal distribution of roles, with a couple of resilient front-liners, some damage specialists and a healer. Not every team could find a good healer... team dynamics were as much about the balance of personalities as the balance of powers".
When a team loses a front-liner it needs a new one.
A group works "as a team, instead of as individuals" against a bronze monster, directed by a leader.

Specialist or generalist. In Rimaros the culture prefers specialists: Jason, with stealth, utility, mobility and summoning powers beside his afflictions, "in Rimaros, you aren't" an affliction specialist, "you're a dabbler; a dilettante".
A Rimaros assessor reads him as "an affliction-using generalist" while another corrects it.
Loot. Teams split loot as a group and keep records for splitting later: Jason "took out a notebook and recorded all the loot for splitting up later".
Choices can reflect need: the team lets Jason and Henrietta split an elemental's loot because each has expensive summoning rituals to pay for.
Rufus gives spare summoning materials to Jason when dividing loot.

Retirement and longevity. Silver-rank arena professionals "keep going until silver-rank longevity is no longer enough, at which point they retire and make their way to gold for the extended life span".
Gary retires after Book 3 to become a full-time weaponsmith.
Silver-rankers in low-magic Greenstone are "semi-retired at best".
Guilds. Guilds are private organisations of adventurers.

During the Book 7 surge, in a city like Livaros "about three in ten adventurers are in a guild. One in ten is in what's considered a high-end guild... Yet guilds are given sixty percent of the quotas to fill".
The Society handles guilds' quotas and leaves them to manage on their own.
Surge quotas. During a surge every adventurer has an action quota; contracts over and above it earn contribution points, tallied on weekly and overall leaderboards with rewards.
Portal users earn more points because of the demand for transport.
Rule of thumb. Rufus's rule of thumb is to handle monsters one rank up only with a good match-up.
Arena sport. Iron-rank monster-hunt events judge teams on performance against identical monsters.
Non-adventurers. Many portal workers "aren't even adventurers and do storage space transport for a living".
Rick Geller's team, with front-liners, damage dealers and a healer.
Jason's first contract logged at the jobs hall desk.
Team Work Saw, whose defender Henry holds a gold-rank converted at the Book 8 Purity attack.
The badge is authority. It is not; the contract carries it.
Higher stars mean more power. Stars measure judgement, not power.
Adventuring is killing for sport. Rufus refuses to work with those who relish it.
Level 1: Jason's one-star iron badge is the starting point; Greenstone's jobs hall changes with a new director.
Level 2: In the Book 7 surge, orders and quotas replace ordinary contracts, and guilds carry most of the load.
Naming and tags. Afflictions and boons appear in brackets with tags: "[Leech Toxin] (affliction, poison, blood, stacking)"; "[Mark of Sin] (affliction, holy)"; "[Resistant] (boon, holy)".
Stacking. Many conditions stack, each "instance" adding to the effect, as for Vulnerable: "Additional instances have a cumulative effect".
Some stacks decay, like Penance, "Stacks drop off over time".
Jason's Sin Eater increases his own resistance to afflictions and gives him Resistant each time he resists or cleanses one.
His Hegemony aura raises allies' resistance and lowers enemies', and lowers it further for each instance of Sin.
In battle only a fraction land: "as many as one in three afflictions were taking hold" against a flesh monster in Book 2, and "almost half" against a lizard after resistance-lowering stacks.

Jason's Feast of Absolution removes "curses, diseases, poisons and unholy afflictions", plus holy afflictions if the target is an ally, from a target other than himself, and it "circumvents all effects that prevent cleansing"; a few chapters later, at Iron 1 (19%), the same spell removes holy and unholy afflictions from an ally or an enemy and "circumvents any resistance or immunity to cleanse effects".
Cleansing triggers other abilities: "Cleansing afflictions has triggered [Sin Eater]".
A cleansing aura, such as Cleansing Breeze, adds resistance to curses, diseases, magic afflictions, poisons and unholy afflictions and negates poisons in the air; it is a holy effect.
Cleanse conditions. Many afflictions are written to resist cleansing: Mark of Sin "cannot be cleansed while target retains any instances of Sin or Legacy of Sin".

A curse can protect another: a patient arrives with two curses, one adding poison to the other, and "the curse that kept making more of the other two couldn't be cleansed until the other curse was cleansed".

Negating immunity. Some afflictions remove an immunity: Weakness of the Flesh "negates immunities to disease and necrotic damage" and that "includes intrinsic immunities, such as from not having a biology or corporeal form".
Blood From a Stone does the same for blood and poison, so "entities without blood can bleed", and Mortality does it for curses, even for the not alive.
Inevitable Demise, an aura Knowledge tried to give him, treated "any affliction immunities, including inherent immunities, as complete resistance".
Healing interaction. Bleeding "soaks up healing, negating its effect" and is removed only after absorbing enough; Leech Toxin reapplies it when negated, "leaving any healing stopped cold".
Weight of Sin deals transcendent damage to anyone subjected to a holy boon, recovery or cleanse effect; Sanction reduces healing.
Hendren's ongoing cleansing powers "could not eliminate holy effects", and he had only one power that could.
Another ability grants resistance to curses, magic and unholy afflictions, and bars unholy boons.
Hegemony is "both a holy and unholy ability at the same time", which fascinates Jason.
Rank gives damage reduction against lower-rank sources.
Sin, Creeping Death and many of Jason's afflictions raise or deal it.

Spell Breaker adds disruptive-force damage, "highly effective against magical defences and incorporeal entities"; Stone Cutter adds resonating-force damage, "highly effective against physical defences".
A defensive gift can reduce disruptive-force damage by a large amount.
An unarmed ability adds resonating-force damage and negates damage from actively intercepted attacks.
Gary's hammer for fighting constructs delivers "a resonating-force explosion" with each hit.
Transcendent damage. "Transcendent damage ignores all forms of physical and magical defence, damage reduction and resistances".
Vincent is astonished at seeing an iron-rank ability deal it.
Jason's Castigate at iron already deals "slight transcendent damage", and execute effects like Verdict scale it with injury.
Definitions from the Book 12 appendix, as of gold rank:
(The full alphabetised list is at.)
Healing beats damage. Bleeding soaks up healing and Leech Toxin reapplies it.
Cleansing is always available. Afflictions like Mark of Sin and Persecution are written to block it.
Immunity is permanent. Weakness of the Flesh, Blood From a Stone and Mortality cancel even intrinsic immunities.
Rank is a wall. Resistance and damage reduction from rank can be bypassed by transcendent damage.
Level 1: Early iron-rank afflictions are described plainly, like Vulnerable's "All resistances are reduced".
Later versions gain extra clauses, such as the cleanse restriction and the intrinsic-immunity text.
Level 2: A speaker in Book 13 says Bussinger's Tribulation Lightning purges her own afflictions at the cost of harming her.
Level 3: By the end of Book 12 Jason's ability set is built around holy-tagged transcendent effects, such as Penance, Weight of Sin and Sanction.
Quintessence. Quintessence is "kind of like chunks of essence" and "gets used a lot more" than essences: "Ritual magic, alchemy, weapon forging".
It appears as small gems named for their theme: dark quintessence is "small black gems".
Water quintessence forms when magic-rich water from an astral space reaches the sea and condenses "huge quantities of magically-imbued water into a little crystal".
Villages along the coast live by finding it.
Gary says he goes "through quintessence by the pile" for weapons and armour.
A quintessence gem can be used directly in an item: a bracelet "keeps the wearer cool and refreshed" with a water gem, and a gem refills its energy.
A quintessence pile cannot be made into an essence.
Spirit coins. A spirit coin is a crystal in the colour of a rank; "the iron-rank coin had the metal-grey colour of iron but was actually made of crystal".
Eaten, it "dissolved with an intense fizzing sensation... tangy and energetic" and restores power.
Ranked people "sustain themselves on spirit coins and go without food entirely".
A coin an hour or so can replenish reserves, with no food for a day or more, and captors give an unconscious captive a coin to eat to keep him healthy.
Coins are grown on farms, where "special moulds cause magic to crystallise", and changes in ambient magic can ruin whole batches.
A vehicle runs on coins fed into a slot.
The currency role is in Economy_and_Money.md; the exchange rates are "a full hundred lesser coins to one iron-rank coin, after which denominations went up in multiples of ten".
Spirit coins and rank. Eating a coin of one's own rank, or ten of one rank lower, restores recovery in low-magic zones.
A coin can briefly boost attributes to offset rank disparity, but it "will leave you weaker once the strength fades".
Potions. A recovery potion restores health, stamina and mana; "until the remnant magic fully dissipates, consuming further health, stamina or mana potions will result in toxic side-effects".
Potions come in ranks: Jason's first is a bronze-rank, rare Recovery Potion.
Healers' patients are limited by cost: both ritual magic and alchemy have ways to heal, "but the cost and expertise required placed both out of the reach for most people".

Jory's "true calling was alchemy", and his research is to make products cheaper and simpler: "If I can make alchemical products affordable to everyone, not only can it help a huge number of people, but it will open up huge new markets".
Alchemy and weapon forging use quintessence.
Alchemists belong to the Alchemy Association, which Jory joins alongside the Adventure Society.
Alchemy sits beside medicine as an everyday tool: the shaving cream Jason mentions came from "an alchemist friend".
Farrah and Clive see "interdisciplinary crossover" between formations and artifice.
Clive mentions "some rather sophisticated artifice" used to tamper with carriages.
The Artifice Association sells good kitchen devices such as stand mixers.
Skilled people mix disciplines: a friend of Clive's has "solid ritual magic, a bit of artifice" and upgraded a mirage chamber.
Crafting. Monster materials are crafting inputs: snakeskin and dark quintessence are crafting materials. Gary makes weapons and armour.
Magic craftspeople range from leatherworkers and weapon-smiths to engravers and alchemists.
Growth items. A growth item gains forms and powers as its rank rises when fed the right materials. Emir's cloud palace "is a growth item".

Jason's cloud flask is "iron rank [growth], legendary", bound to him, and its upgrade to bronze needs 1000 bronze air quintessence, 1000 bronze water quintessence, 200 bronze dimension quintessence and 10,000 bronze spirit coins.
Legendary growth weapons come in matched sets.

Soul-bound items. A soul-bound growth item "cannot be used by anyone else" and "tends to take on" its owner's properties as it advances; Clive says that "if you meet someone who seems like a good person but has a hideous and twisted soul-bound item, stay clear".
Emir's cloud palace, "outrageously grandiose, yet welcoming and beautiful", reflects him.
Soul-bound items "are rare, even compared to other growth items. The advancement requirements are usually quite prohibitive".

Communication. Long-distance speech runs through the Magic Society's water link chambers: "Communicating through watery clones was the most accessible form of long-distance communication and a major use for the magical stone that Greenstone exported".
The people on the other end appear as water clones "indistinguishable from her actual parents to the eye", although magical senses show them to be projections.
In a surge the Adventure Society takes over the links and cancels bookings.
A carried device like "a water link chamber you carry around in your pocket" is mentioned as a communication network item.
Other tools. Crystal wash is an odourless cleaner that "clears off everything"; its absence is a running problem.
Recording crystals capture images, messages and fights.
Dimensional storage includes bags; Jason's inventory has forty spaces, with stacking.
Low-magic zones. Coin farms work only where magic is stable: "No activity, no life. Very stable ambient magic".
Divine supply. A church can supply healing essences and stones.
Prices. Coins bought in bulk go through brokers; an adventurer can be paid in coins up to an awakening stone for a contract.
Hydra whip and other loot. Monster-part weapons keep some properties: a hydra whip "had the hydra's property of regeneration".
Bracelet with water quintessence.
Skimmer powered by coins.
Cloud palace and cloud flask.
Jory's clinic, an alchemy lab and medical clinic in one building.
Quintessence can replace essences. It cannot.
Healing potions are always safe to chain. They cause toxic side effects until the remnant magic dissipates.
Soul-bound items are interchangeable. They are bound and reflect the owner.
Level 1: Greenstone's market for essences and stones fell to an all-time low after the astral space was plundered.
Level 3: In Book 12 Travis offers to build weapons for the cloud flask, saying he has "done weapons for your cloud flask before, but that was years ago".

sec: 7. Item types and where they are described
claim: Fundamental Realm Authority Token — A transcendent-rank token bound to Jason that opens gates to the fundamental realm —../09_Items_and_Artefacts/Tokens_Stones_and_Relics.md

Astral spaces. Farrah: "Astral spaces are pretty common, but normally they're sealed off and you need magic to track one down and break in. Being naturally open like this is rare, especially with so many apertures".
Greenstone's river comes out of a large aperture.

An aperture connects a place on the physical world to the astral space; an astral space may have many apertures, and the mayor of one town notes theirs is "only one of many places with an aperture leading to that astral space".
An astral space can be a rainforest island chain, with a sun that "just moving around on a circuit in the sky" and no night.
It can be far smaller than the world it is attached to: "the astral space is only a fraction of the size of the world it's attached to".
Expeditions enter through the aperture, making camp, searching in teams and retreating through it for triage.

Why they are attached. Clive: "Astral spaces form attached to worlds, without which they immediately break down. Without a real world to anchor them, they cannot exist. But if an astral space is given the ability to sustain itself, even for just a brief period, the Builder can take it and anchor it to the world the Builder is creating from stolen parts".
The Builder's process preserved the astral space at the cost of catastrophic destruction to the physical reality.
Surges. "Every ten years there's a massive increase in the spawn rate of monsters. All across the world, all at the same time. Whole villages evacuate to fortified towns".
The last one was eleven years earlier; "it's never exactly ten years. It's been as little as eight or as many as thirteen. The last few have all come pretty late".
Most of the delta's population "comes into the city during monster surges".

The Book 7 surge is "some five years overdue, during which time monster activity had gradually increased. Once the surge proper began, it was expected to be more brutal and last longer than any in history".
During a surge adventurers earn contribution points instead of direct payment, and guilds use it to scout talent.
Proto-astral spaces (Earth). A proto-astral space is "unstable dimensional pockets attached to the world".
Their usual duration is "forty-three hours"; an anomalous one in Book 4 lasted "less than a second" and was the size and shape of a person, though its rated strength still registered above five.

The aperture to one "wasn't visible to the naked eye, although magical senses made it extremely easy to see. It was a more tenuous bridge across dimensional boundaries than a normal aperture and appeared... as if it might collapse at any moment".
Entering one is announced by a System message: "The ambient magical saturation has increased. Your recovery rates will remain at normal levels without spirit coin consumption".
Spirit coins cannot be formed in them: "Earth doesn't have the magic and coin formation takes months, so you can't do it in the proto-astral spaces".

Transformation zones (Earth). In the Russian city of Kostroma the whole city "was sealed off in a dome", actually a sphere that extended underground; "forty-three hours after the sphere moved into place, it vanished, revealing a city vastly changed".
The changes remake the area "in the image of worlds used as patterns when the original Builder created this universe".
Buildings look weathered with years of age.

On Earth many normal-ranked people were transformed into other races in accordance with the zone they were in, humans becoming "leonids, celestines and other races native to neither Earth nor Pallimustus".

Zones as spaces to be claimed. A transformation zone that Jason enters contains a genesis space, which his System names: "You have established a spirit domain. Expanding your spirit domain will define and stabilise unstable genesis space but trigger anomalous reactions from genesis space outside the spirit domain".
Territories are claimed by defeating anomalies and then a final one: "You have overtaken a genesis space territory and purged all anomalous elements". See Monsters.md for the anomalies.
Pallimustus has no such need, so the dimensional rupture there required "another hand to trigger the transformation zone".

Jason's three zones. In the first he "had broken into a zone already in place" and it forcibly evolved an outworlder power into Spiritual Domain; in the second he could reshape it from the start and raised the base level of magic on Earth, so that "magic no longer manifested in proto-astral spaces before spilling into the world"; the third is on Pallimustus.

The special zone. The System describes the Book 11 zone: "This special transformation zone must be unified to restore stability, reintegrate it with physical reality and re-establish an astral space", unified by "claiming all non-central territories".
Each territory is claimed by eliminating a final anomaly, and if several are present it "must be ceded to one individual through conflict or forfeit".
Nitra. A transformation zone at Nitra in Slovakia forms as a "glimmering dome several kilometres across" that stays closed for days.
The Chinese forces under Li Li Mei claim a site around it.
Low-magic zones. In a low-magic area, "consuming a spirit coin of your rank or ten spirit coins of one rank lower will restore your recovery rates to normal for eight hours".
The desert's water-source astral space in Book 1, an island-chain rainforest; more in 06_Places/Astral_Spaces/.
Kostroma in Book 5, the first transformation zone, 43 hours long.
Bankstown, Sydney, a zone with lava streams.
Nitra, a Book 5 to 6 dome.
The Cardinas zone in Book 11.
Astral spaces are the same as other worlds. They are small pockets attached to a world.
Proto-astral spaces last forever. They last about forty-three hours.
A surge is exactly ten years. It ranges from eight to thirteen.
Level 2: The first zones on Earth are 43 hours long and remake places in the pattern of other worlds.

Level 3: After Jason's second zone, "The base level of magic had risen; magic no longer manifested in proto-astral spaces before spilling into the world. He had begun a new age of magic, where monsters and essences manifested directly in the world".
Aura sense. A new iron-ranker gains the ability to sense auras.

Jason's first impression of other ranked people is a feeling of danger, which Rufus explains is "our auras. Now that you're iron rank, you can sense them", and which gets more reliable as he learns to tell the difference "between a monster, an essence user and a regular person".
The sense is "not completely reliable" because "some monsters can hide their auras. People can too, if they have an aura power".

Ordinary people are "faint, barely detectable, while those with essences were much clearer"; a village normally has one or two with an essence, and a full-set iron-ranker "radiated out like a beacon".

The three controls. Farrah teaches Jason to control his aura "in three ways": "projecting your aura and restraining it", then "using your aura to suppress the auras of other people", which is "harder than the others", to be left alone "until you reach a certain level of proficiency".
Projection is "pushing your aura out to affect people"; restraining is "drawing it in, whether to hide it, or just not be rude".
Everyone projects until they learn not to: "It's what makes people with no aura control easy to read".
Later the text repeats that "all aura control techniques were variations or extensions of those three".
Why it matters. Anyone with a perception power will eventually see auras clearly, so an uncontrolled aura reads like signs, including location and emotions, and "know when you lie".

The skill with which an aura is controlled "is how adventurers make their first impressions on one another. If you can't do it properly, people won't take you seriously. Excellent aura manipulation marks you as an adventurer of training and distinction".
Farrah calls the lack of an aura ability a serious gap: "anyone who hits bronze rank and can't manage their aura is a second-rate adventurer".
A gold-ranker's aura. At gold an uncontrolled aura is dangerous to normal people: "If you reach gold rank and can't control your aura properly, you can hurt normal people just by going near them".
Such people are required to wear a suppressor: Farrah once saw "a gold ranker who forgot to put on an aura suppressor before going to a market. People were passed out, bleeding out their ears".

Jason, in Book 4, slowly unleashes his aura in a room: "Normal humans couldn't detect auras unless they were projected in a specific way. It was a simple use of basic projection control... a tool that essence users employed to intimidate normals".
Higher-rank auras can be pointed at lower-rank ones: a bronze-rank woman suppresses Jason's with her own, which is "the very height of rudeness".
A silver-ranker's weight can be felt without being a suppressing force.
Blending in. A gold-ranker can use aura control to pass through a crowd unnoticed, and a high-end silver can do the same.
The technique blends projection and retraction to merge the aura into the ambient magic, with delicate suppression to blunt others' aura senses.
Normal people "were aura blind unless someone with aura control didn't want them to be".

Jason's inspirations are Farrah's orthodox teaching, his own experience, Vermillion's use of aura on normals, the Mirror King's aura that "had felt like a part of the world around it", and Shade's masking.

Farrah mentions aura suppressors; a thief's methods include "aura masking"; an aura mask is breached by using essence abilities or failing to keep a strong aura suppressed; aura masking will not work against a tracking effect on the aura.
A suppression collar can negate a target's powers; Jason is able to "completely negate the effects of an iron-rank suppression collar" after practice, and holds off a bronze one for a few moments.

Silver and levitation. "Levitation, Jason had discovered, was a perk of reaching silver-rank. It was an intrinsic property of a silver-rank soul, allowing the aura it projected to physically affect the environment".
Farrah warns that it is "not even a practical ability. It requires intense concentration, has minimal effect, and is easy to disrupt with just some basic aura suppression".
At silver it was "mostly just a power to levitate that helped their increasingly heavy bodies walk on weaker surfaces or even water".
Aura signatures. An aura has a signature that places can record: Emir's cloud palace stores Jason's signature in its registry and cannot let him in when it changes.
A soul crest carries a unique imprint on the aura that stays the same even when the aura changes, "impossible to track or falsify through even the strongest magic".
Aura powers. Some abilities are auras (Hegemony, Cleansing Breeze), which are a different thing from the aura itself: they are passive effects projected around the user.
"An aura power common to the force confluence famously allowed auras to move things physically", and Jason's cannot.
Perception and silver. Farrah says her perception power does not improve her aura sense until silver rank.
Monsters. "Higher-rank monsters can" manipulate their auras; at low ranks the most to expect is "a few stealthy monsters that restrain their auras to hide better".

Transcendent echo. Soul damage from gods can change an aura: after multiple divine presences press on him, Jason's "aura has been damaged by the direct, concerted focus of multiple transcendent-level entities", the recovery refines it, and it now carries "an echo of transcendent power".
Jason's Interface uses titles to translate soul scars into game terms.

Resolute raises resistance to suppression from higher-ranked auras; Indomitable enhances resistance and "ignores rank disparity", and adds a resistance bonus to allies in his aura; Spirit Warrior increases both suppressive force and resistance, lets him resist other magical suppression, and lets him "attack their soul directly" after fully suppressing their aura; Godless Prophet records the refinement after gods press on him. Each changes his aura signature.
Rank disparity. Aura strength is "the inherently superior strength of higher-rank auras", which some of Jason's titles do not cancel.
Normals cannot feel them. Normals can sense strong, directed auras on some level but are "aura blind" unless the wielder allows it.
Suppressing an aura is simple. Farrah calls it the hardest of the three controls.
Level 1: In Book 3 Jason refines his suppression until he can hold off an iron-rank collar entirely.
Level 2: After his Book 4 return to Earth, Jason rebuilds his aura control from scratch to use on normal people with "art and finesse".
Level 3: The Numen gift in Book 12 makes his avatar immune to rank suppression and lets him negate aura abilities by fully suppressing the user's aura.
It is the third kind of non-living magic Rufus lists, after essences and quintessence.
What a stone does. Each stone's description says the same thing: "Awakens an essence ability", with the requirement "Unawakened essence ability".
Jason is shown a count of how many abilities he still has to awaken, such as "You have 10 unawakened essence abilities".
Stones can also be used in other kinds of magic: "sometimes awakening stones get used as part of very powerful rituals", as the cult did with its feast stones in the sacrifice chamber.
What decides the ability. Farrah: "the biggest determinate of what ability you get is the essence it comes from".

A stone has a theme, and the theme sets the range of powers: a feast stone is "related to the concept of a feast, but that can manifest in any of hundreds of powers", which Farrah corrects to "thousands".
This is why Farrah and Rufus advise taking every essence before using stones: otherwise "your abilities will lack focus".
Rarity and specificity. "The more rare an awakening stone is, the more specific the powers".
A common stone "can give you any ability the rarest could", it just draws from a larger pool; "rare stones don't give out better abilities, just more specific ones".
The stones people seek are those with a desirable specialty, and "stones with desirable specialties tend to be the most expensive".
A mid-rarity stone is "almost always a useful utility power".
A high-rarity stone is "more specialised" and restricts the possible abilities to just one or two types.

Grading. The Magic Society grades stones on a scale of one to five stars "based on how frequently they are known to appear world-wide", working with brokers and the Adventure Society; Jason's ability also sorts them into five stages of rarity: common (one star), uncommon (two stars), up to epic (four stars, "the second highest rarity") and legendary.
In the Adventure Society's wording, a stone of the apocalypse is "unranked, legendary" and a stone of omens "unranked, epic".
Using one. The stone melts into the user's hand or arm and sinks in without fanfare, and Jason's system confirms "You have awakened the blood essence ability [Leech Bite]".
Most people need a ritual for each stone, and a person with a whole row "going through a half-dozen rituals would take hours".
Clive's essence ability, Enact Ritual, makes drawing and performing the circles more convenient.
Clive draws the circle and completes the ritual when a team member uses an uncommon stone of preparation.
Hunger afterwards. A stone of the feast leaves Jason ravenous: "I think the stone of the feast made it worse". The cure is a spirit coin.
Jason's first stone is the "Awakening Stone of the Stars".
A shopping list includes awakening stones of the eyes, the hand and the foot.
Neil and Jason select awakening stones of the avatar, and Humphrey selects an awakening stone of rebirth.
One speaker mentions an awakening stone of defiance.

Tendencies of a theme. The text gives these: eyes "a good shot at giving a perception power"; hand awakens empty-hand abilities and attacks; foot, unarmed attacks and movement abilities; sky, a very good chance of a flight power, though "it could just as easily give you a special attack effective against enemies in the air"; purgation, "almost certainly some kind of cleansing ability"; magus, "a common awakening stone, especially with humans... almost guaranteed a spell, which humans rarely awakened, with an outside chance of a coveted summoning or familiar power"; omens, a hope for an aura power.
Human aptitude. Humans have an aptitude for special attacks and rarely awaken spells without a magus stone.
One aura only. A person can have just one aura ability; the stone that would give a second does not work.
A tablet can remove an existing aura ability.

Knowledge sends Jason two: a Divine Awakening Stone of Inevitability, to bestow an aura power (the ability is [Inescapable Doom] in one line and [Inevitable Demise] in another), and a Divine Awakening Stone of Persistence, to bestow a specific spell, with a Soul-Purgation Tablet to make room.
Jason shuts the case, calling it "a shiny red apple" and a poison pill.
A god can take back what it gave: Jason says "the idea of some god repossessing my magic powers doesn't appeal".

Great astral beings' stones. "The stones the astral beings produce aren't divine stones that the astral beings can revoke. They're just ordinary awakening stones whose aspect aligns with the great astral being in question".
Relatively common from the Reaper and the Celestial Book, not from the World-Phoenix.

Rare means better. Farrah and Rufus both deny it.
A stone can be aimed. "There are no guarantees when it comes to awakening powers, not even with the rarest of stones".
Clive: "I'm just managing expectations".
A stone saves you from needing a full set. Rufus's advice is to take all four essences first.
Stones are only for abilities. They also fuel rituals.
The Adventure Society raised the bounty on Jason to a four-star stone for each person on the team that caught him, with a cap of six after people formed giant groups.
The Society gives out stones for exceptional service, rarely, and as rewards for contributions in open contracts.
A Geller family tradition supplies scions "with enough awakening stones to get started".
As a rule, "we don't give out awakening stones to people for killing monsters above their rank", so that people are not tempted to jump ranks.
In a joking exchange, one speaker admits to using a stone of defiance and a companion teases that they expected an ability from a chef-type essence.

Arrival. Farrah explains that "once you use your third essence, a fourth one manifests itself on the spot" and that confluences are "a result of the three essences you already have"; her own fire, earth and potent gave the volcano essence.
Confluences "only manifest after three essences are used", and cannot be found loose: "You can't find a volcano essence anywhere".

The scene. When Jason uses his third essence, three shimmering cubes rise from his torso and merge into one new cube; the System tells him the "confluence of your essences has produced the doom essence", which he "may claim or reject", and that a refused confluence "will not be available to you again".
Rufus's practical advice is that refusing means one "can only replace it with a normal essence" and "I promise you that is not the way to go".
Only the clergy refuse, because their gods give them divine versions of regular essences.
A person can look an essence up to see what combinations are known and which are restricted.
Jason's dark, blood and sin is found there and produces doom, which is not restricted.
Clive can name a result from memory, as he does for swift, balance and wind.
The Society's common-combinations list is the basis for many choices, such as Ian's ministration confluence.
A larger list of "thousands of known essence combinations" is offered for sale to Jason by the Network's envoy.
Mystic is common because "so many combinations produce it" and because "a lot of useful abilities come out of the mystic essence".
Undeath is produced by "a wide variety of combinations, almost all of which involve the death essence".
Garuda has at least two routes, might, swift and bird, and might and wing, which Jason secures instead of the plan to give Taika renewal and the immortal confluence.
Confluence abilities come late. It is "quite unusual to awaken the confluence essence abilities first", and some advocates of a theory say people with a very strong sense of self do it.
Kylie's vision confluence lets her awaken a perception power from each essence, "where other essence users only had the one".
An aura power common to the force confluence is able to move things physically with an aura, which is unusual.

Adventurer's confluences. Farrah calls chimera "an adventurer's confluence", unsuited to a civilian such as Kaito, who is given a combination of common essences: vehicle, wind and swift, forming the soaring confluence, a known non-combat flight combination.
Surprising results from the user. Greg's magitech confluence did not look like the Network's high-tech magitech users; Jason and Ketevan remark that he ended "all steampunk Tesla".

Rare essences, common results. Sword, myriad and adept give master as readily as sword, swift and adept, in a different style: Lance, a spell-using elf, shares the confluence with Valdis, who relies on special attacks.

Erika is given feast, knife and dance, producing bounty, a food-magic confluence, and Yumi takes blood, flesh and bone, which give the avatar confluence and let her remake her body into an idealised younger one.
Jason's two sets for the former Engineers of Ascension are sun, blood and life (avatar, "about as perfect an anti-vampire set as you'll find") or gun, hand and adept (master).

Further named confluences in the text include Medusa (Jason's joke about a hair essence plus snake and earth), phoenix (Humphrey's sister), and the lotus set Jason imagines for a Japanophile friend.
People do pick a set to aim at a confluence, with the Society list as guide.
Refusing the confluence frees the slot for a better one. Rufus: "I promise you that is not the way to go".

A confluence guarantees a role. Clive taught Jason to shape a power set "by aiming for powers within a certain scope" rather than seeking specific powers, and the same confluence plays differently by user (see section 3).

The fixed pairing ends. Rufus is told that essence combinations have "only one potential confluence" and "before the Cosmic Throne was sundered, things were different. More flexible", that an essence combination could once "produce different confluences, from person to person".

After the sundering, "the Celestial Book locked off essence combinations" and, if Jason repairs the throne, "all those restrictions will be undone"; the restrictions "are already starting to unravel".
The first reported case is Emi, whose vast, myriad and harmonic should produce unity and instead give resonant.

A speaker in Book 12 reports that "the previously fixed essence combinations are starting to add variety to the confluence essences they produce", and that some people refuse the confluence, "especially now that the combinations are becoming less reliable".

Gary's Cup of Heroes. When Gary becomes a demigod his essences are replaced by divine ones, and his forge confluence by a Demigod essence, with abilities replaced to match. The effect on others is not shown.

The old magic. Craig Vermillion: "Magic has always been a difficult and esoteric thing. Some five centuries ago, a new kind of magic appeared. People with no connection to the old ways could suddenly wield a variety of easy-to-use mystical powers. At that time, they were a limited threat. They were collected into various secret societies around the world, hoarding their knowledge".
Tiers. The shared numeric rank system runs from zero up: "Whether you call them tiers, categories, realms, or ranks, like you, the same numbers are recognised across the board".
Tier zero is people without enough magic to "cross the first, transformative threshold".
Blood servants can reach the first or second tier temporarily by ingesting vampire blood.

Vermillion says he and Jason are "tier two of five", that he has heard of tier-four Cabal figures who "entered forms of hibernation, hidden away for centuries", and that the fifth tier is "the limit of mortal power".
In Network usage the ranks are called categories after spirit coin colours: category one is iron, two bronze, three silver. See Ranks_and_Advancement.md.

"The grid infrastructure isn't like a normal formation array of permanent ritual circles. Each node is enormous and not made from a ritual circle at all. It's like the landscape is somehow operating as a series of interconnected rituals, creating a magical array from the natural features of the world itself. We're talking about nodes the size of cities, with elements made up of mountains, hills and rivers to form a magical array covering the entire planet".
Its "express purpose is to identify and monitor dimensional spaces".
It is "designed to be accessible to anyone with the requisite knowledge", so that once Jason knows about it he may tap into it himself.
It registers events by category: an incident in Book 4 "registered as being above category five".
A local branch once hid the Saint-Étienne astral space by disabling the Grid in that area and "claiming that there was an infrastructure collapse".

Where magic comes from. Dawn explains: "The link between worlds has been siphoning off magic from Pallimustus to this world for centuries. It was slow, at first, but the rate of transfer has been rapidly escalating over the last century and a half. Each proto-space that breaks down without the anchor creatures being destroyed deposits its magic into your world... after centuries, the magical density of your world has started to rise. This strengthens the link, which feeds the loop".

The founders of the Grid and the Network "failed to prepare a response to proto-spaces appearing deep in the oceans", so the Network "slows the rate at which your world's magical density has risen" without stopping it.
Supplies. Earth has no spirit coin farms: "Earth doesn't have the magic and coin formation takes months, so you can't do it in the proto-astral spaces".
Quintessence is called affinity gems: "We call them affinity gems. I'm pretty sure the Network is the main supplier".
The Network gives its executive staff essences to reach category one and reserves cores for frontline staff.
Magical technology exists, built on leaning "on the magic as little as possible. Let the technology do the work and use magic to skip over the places where the tech would otherwise bottleneck".
Characters on Earth. Essence users on Earth are mostly category one to three in Book 4.

Low-magic rule. Entering the vicinity of a proto-astral aperture raises ambient magic enough that "your recovery rates will remain at normal levels without spirit coin consumption"; outside such places Earth's magic is thin.
Core use as policy. Network members are given cores according to role and rank rather than by ability.
Training divergence. The Network's own training is human-derived; Jason and Farrah introduce training "from the ground up" in Book 5.
Kostroma, the first transformation zone, in.
Nitra, Slovakia, a zone at the end of Book 5.
The Quilido Procedure, Book 13's cure for core taint.
Earth has no magic. It has a trickle, increasingly large.
The Network can contain it. Jason concludes that the Network's mission of containment "was completely stuffed from the start" because the oceans hide leaks, and Dawn agrees.
Tier five is a myth. Vermillion has "never seen proof" of it.
Level 2: In Book 5, grid failures and monster waves begin; the Network becomes publicly known as the Global Defense Network. Zones such as Kostroma remake places.

Level 3: After Jason's second zone, "the base level of magic had risen; magic no longer manifested in proto-astral spaces before spilling into the world. He had begun a new age of magic, where monsters and essences manifested directly in the world".
Many normal-rank people on Earth are transformed into other races.
By Book 13 the Asano clan's training and the Quilido Procedure give it influence over national essence-user programmes.
The full set of essences the Magic Society knows is in its living document.
The wiki's fuller lists of essences, confluences and combinations are in Wiki_Reference_Lists.md, with a cross-reference to the first book line for each entry found in the text.
Where the wiki gives a rarity, it agrees with the text so far: sin is Legendary, renewal is Epic (the text's "second-highest rarity") and rune and vast are among the highest.
The text uses five stages for stones: common, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary (puts four-star at the "second highest rarity").
