Names and concepts. An essence name is a concept, not a promise of power: the bird essence might give "the power to talk to birds" rather than a combat power.
Same essence, different user. The vehicle essence gives drones to Kaito and a conjured limousine to Wesley Asano and a helicopter to another.
Level 3: Gary's essences are replaced by divine versions (Divine Hammer, Divine Fire, Divine Iron) and his forge confluence by Demigod.

What an essence is. Rufus lists three non-living manifestations of magic: essences, "the most powerful manifestation" and "also, the rarest", then quintessence, "kind of like chunks of essence", and awakening stones.
A pile of quintessence cannot be used as an essence; "there's always some crackpot who claims to have figured it out, but it isn't possible".
Clive's explanation is that the astral is "the source of all magic", that some worlds soak up a lot of it, and that this world's magic takes forms such as essences, stones, quintessence and monsters.
Essences appear as cubes or crystals: Jason's blood essence is a red cube whose slick surface looks wet but is dry and warm; his sin essence is a white and gold cube.
Where they come from. Magic "just starts manifesting all over the place" in a world as rich in it as this one. They are also bought and sold.

Jason trades a rat essence to a broker for two awakening stones, brokers run regular essence and stone auctions, and after the Book 2 expedition the market price of essences and stones reached "an all-time low".
Families pool money to buy essence sets for promising young people, and criminals buy powerful ones.
Dean's family could "afford a full set of essences" for him from a living made with water quintessence.
Absorption. Absorbing an essence is done by an essence ritual.
Farrah offers to perform one for Jason, and a ritual is ordinarily required for stones too.
The prompt that follows asks whether to absorb and reports "You have absorbed 2 of 4 essences". Absorption is painful.

Jason passes out for the first (the dark essence turns to smoke and invades his body), the blood essence melts over his hand and burns into his flesh, and the sin essence fills him like inflating pressure.
Farrah observes that each absorption seems easier and asks whether subjects adapt.
Once absorbed, "an essence cannot be relinquished or replaced".
Five abilities, one awakened. Each essence "imbues 1 awakened essence ability and 4 unawakened essence abilities".
A full set therefore has twenty abilities, and a person "can't even properly progress towards bronze rank until you awaken every essence ability".
Attribute bonding. Each essence bonds to one attribute and raises it from normal to iron: blood to Power, dark to Speed, sin to Recovery and doom to Spirit in Jason's case.
Mastering all of an essence's abilities then raises that attribute.

Order of use. Farrah and Rufus advise using all essences first and stones afterwards, because abilities are shaped by the essences and abilities a person already has; "awaken too many abilities before you have all your essences, and your abilities will lack focus".
The fourth essence. The first three are chosen; the fourth is a confluence and arrives by itself. See Confluences.md.

Jason's message lists the changes: damage reduction against normal-rank sources, increased resistance to normal-rank effects, the ability to sense auras, and the ability to sustain himself with concentrated magic.
The body expels impurities as it moves toward "a state of perfection". See Ranks_and_Advancement.md.
Outworlder absorption. Jason absorbed his first essence "without a ritual" and thinks it was tied to the same power that lets him speak every language.
The ritual knowledge from the skill book tells him a ritual is normally required, "except, he knew from experience that wasn't always true".
Racial difference. Humans "have their essence abilities increase faster than other races".
Abilities and their awakening differ by person as well as race.
Divine essences. Gods give their clergy "divine versions of regular essences", so clergy reject the confluence.
The Healer's church supplies the essences and stones for its healing abilities.
Divine essences come back to the god: when the Builder cult's captives are freed, those with divine essences have the power "returned to their god" and are weaker.
A freed group of cult-held priests who lose divine gifts either join another church or replace them with regular essences.
Ex-clergy stripped of divinely gifted essences suffer "a debilitating imbalance in the body and soul".

Jason refuses divine essences because "the idea of some god repossessing my magic powers doesn't appeal"; Clive adds that great astral beings cannot make essences "the way that gods can" but can make their own stones.

Restricted essences. The Adventure Society keeps a list of essences and combinations "that pose an inherent threat to ordinary people", with the death essence at the top of it by itself, "because it always seems to go wrong".
Membership is impossible with a restricted essence.
The combinations that produce the undeath confluence almost all involve death.
The Magic Society's living document lists every known essence and combination, with restricted ones flagged, and Jason's sin essence is in "the rarest category".
Farrah says the sin essence is in the rarest category.
A rune essence reaches Clive as an "epic four-star essence".
Low-rarity essences are the ones ordinary buyers afford.
The rat essence is "not popular with anyone who could afford to be choosy".

Not all essences are simple. An essence can seem to carry a meaning far from its name: Neil says it takes arrogance to absorb "the essence of defying the gods", and Jason replies that the sin essence is not about defying gods for him.
Jason: dark, blood and sin, giving the doom confluence.
Farrah: fire, earth and potent, giving volcano.
Sophie: swift, balance and wind, giving mystic.
Belinda: magic, trap and adept, giving charlatan.
Clive: magic, rune and balance, giving karmic.
Neil: shield, growth and renewal, giving prosperity.
Essences change who you are. Anisa's church holds that "the essences we use change who we are" and favours only the ones it sees as holy or pure, saying other essences taint the soul.
Rufus's reply is that essence abilities "aren't inherently good or bad. Like a sword, they can be used to oppress or protect"; accountability lies with the wielder.
He allows that the restricted list covers "rare and extreme cases".
An American religious type told Jason "Essences are god's test to see who is worthy of the power".
Rarer means better. For stones, Rufus says "rare stones don't give out better abilities, just more specific ones"; the same applies in spirit to essences, whose power comes from concept and user.
You can make an essence from quintessence. Farrah calls it impossible.
A confluence can be found loose. "You can't find a volcano essence anywhere".

Level 2: Jason offers awakening stones to former Engineers of Ascension members, saying there are enough in his stock to send two of them off "with a full set of powers", and notes that rushing is not ideal.

What a summoned familiar is. Clive's explanation: "Summoning a familiar is like deliberately creating a monster. A chunk of magic is brought into our world and forms a body. What makes it different from a monster is that it also summons a creature from the deep astral. Such entities are purely magical, like a soul. They normally can't exist in physical reality, any more than we can exist in the astral. But they inhabit the body you've made. Give it a mind, and stability. So it doesn't break down and go berserk".
An outworlder's body is akin to a monster's or a summoned familiar's: "physical substance forged out of raw magic".
Summoned familiars from the deep astral are "an endless supply of bizarre and terrifying horrors".

A call-type power works differently: "a creature that has an affinity to that call will come and form a bond with the person. Less costly than summoning, but if that kind of familiar dies, you can't just summon it again".
Summoned versus bonded. A bonded familiar survives its owner's death; a summoned one does not, but a summoned familiar "can disappear into the summoner's body, which bonded familiars can't".
A bonded familiar can be sensed at all times, a summoned one only while subsumed in the summoner.
Humphrey and his dragon Stash "could always sense one another... over any distance".

Bonding is more reliable: "when going for a bonded familiar instead of a summoned one, things are much more likely to go your way, if you prepare accordingly", and "as close as you'll come to a guaranteed result with any awakening stone".

The ritual. To summon Jason's first familiar, he draws the circle with blood and magical materials while the rest watch; the circle and the pool of blood vanish into the floor "drawn back through the astral channel created by the summoning".
Each rank-up needs a resummoning with materials suited to the new rank: Jason brings bronze-rank materials in advance and two sets for each familiar in case a vessel is destroyed.
The text lists a requirement for Shade's bronze resummoning as 343 dark quintessence gems.
Other circles can be simple: "Most people just need a circle of good old salt".
Who can have one. "You can only awaken that kind of essence ability if you already understand ritual magic".
Jason's ritual skill book gave "the bare minimum" to be a proper ritual magician and is "how you awakened a familiar summoning power".
Rufus has no summoning power because his obsession is swordsmanship.
Subsuming. A summoned familiar "can temporarily disperse its body and place its spirit inside the summoner".
Belinda's lantern familiar Shimmer sits in her eyes, turning them silver; purple eyes mark another's summoned familiar.
Belinda's familiar can see hidden enemies from her eyes and fire disruptive-force beams from them.

Summons that are not familiars. A temporary summon "was not a summoned familiar but a temporary summons, like Gary's forge golem or Farrah's magma elemental. It would only last for a limited time, but he could afford to risk it in ways that he couldn't with a familiar".
Farrah and Gary "call up short-lived monsters" as essence powers, and "Rituals that are also essence powers tend to be quick and dirty".
Examples from Jason's set include Cloak of Night, Hand of the Reaper and Blade of Doom, listed as conjurations in the Book 12 appendix.
Swarm familiars are rare. Rick: "Swarm-type familiars are really rare. I've seen more dragon and phoenix familiars".
Many familiars. Henrietta keeps three summoned familiars inside her body and a fourth, a phoenix, bonded.
Jason and Clive each have summoned familiars.
Jason's Shadow of the Hegemon goes from three bodies at iron to seven, thirty-one, then two hundred and eleven at gold, with new traits at each rank.
Sanguine Horror gains a worm-that-walks form at bronze, robes that boost drain at silver and the ability to exceed mass limits at gold.
Avatar of Doom gains detonating orbs, afflicting orbs and affliction clouds.
Appearance echoes the owner. Clive notes that Jason's two familiars "are both reflective of your appearance" in his cloak.
Apocalypse beast familiars. Jason's first, the Sanguine Horror, is described as "an apocalypse beast", and Clive notes Jason "is not the only adventurer to have an apocalypse beast familiar".
Powers not tied to a familiar. Neil's summon "would only last for a limited time" and works best when fighting alone.
Jason's three familiars. Colin, the first, is the Sanguine Horror, summoned in Book 1 and described as "a swarm of leeches".
Shade, a shadow familiar, belongs to the dark essence.
Gordon, whose beams and later butterflies mark him, belongs to Avatar of Doom.
Humphrey's dragon Stash. A bonded familiar.
Belinda's lantern. A summoned astral lantern familiar called Shimmer.
Henrietta's phoenix. The only bonded familiar among four she has, "rare and elusive".
A familiar will eat you. When Colin's swarm crawls into Jason's wounds, Gary asks if it is eating him; Farrah says, "It's his familiar".
Summoned means disposable. It costs ritual materials at each rank-up.
Bonded is better. Jason's summoned familiars "had many advantages over a bonded familiar like Humphrey's, but a bond had its own advantages".
Level 1: In Book 2 Jason awakens Shadow of the Reaper and Hand of the Reaper from stones of the Reaper and Avatar of Doom as his final doom ability.
Level 2: At gold Jason's blood familiar appears in a blood clone form, four copies of a red-eyed Jason, below diamond rank unable to be permanent.
Level 3: The Palanquin gift in Book 12 lets Jason's familiars become vehicles: the dark familiar forms transport, the blood familiar reinforces it and the doom familiar adds offence and defence.
The author notes that the list "is written for brevity (believe it or not) rather than accuracy or comprehensiveness".

claim: The sheet and the ability pages differ on types: the sheet lists Cloak of Night and Hand of the Reaper as special abilities, while the ability pages call both conjurations, as the original screen for Cloak of Night does.
Midnight Eyes — See through darkness — Sense magic — Read auras — Diminish light sources in view

Hand of the Reaper — A shadow arm inflicting Creeping Death — Also Rigor Mortis; a second arm — Also Weakness of the Flesh; numerous arms, including at range from shadows — More arms, further away; armed with conjured weapons
Cloak of Night — A cloak that manipulates light and weight — Intercepts projectiles — Allows flight and minor space distortion — A void portal for extreme ongoing mana cost
Path of Shadows — Teleport through a visible shadow — Portals across regional distances — Continental distances — Global distances

Shadow of the Hegemon — Shadow familiar with three bodies — Seven bodies; minor physical force; dimensional storage — Thirty-one bodies; summoner can share non-combat powers — Two hundred and eleven bodies; bodies serve as beacons for the summoner's aura

Blood Harvest — Drain health, stamina and mana from an enemy corpse; only targets with blood — All enemy corpses in a wide area — Blood Frenzy for each corpse, then Blood of the Immortal — Strength of My Enemies, then Endless Power
Leech Bite — Bleeding; drains life from bleeding targets — Leech Toxin — Tainted Meridians — Thief of Life
Haemorrhage — Bleeding and Sacrificial Victim — Necrotoxin — Blood From a Stone — Exsanguination
Feast of Blood — Drain life from bleeding targets — Additional life per poison — Variant with more targets, longer cooldown — Blood Glutton for each victim

Sanguine Horror — Summon a sanguine horror familiar — A worm-that-walks form — Conjures robes enhancing drain and regeneration; can spend its own biomass to heal the summoner — Can exceed normal mass limits through life drain
Punish — Necrotic damage and Sin — Price of Absolution — Wages of Sin on those with Sin; against those with Penance, transcendent damage and more Penance — Thief of Spirit
Castigate — Brand, Sin and Mark of Sin — Weight of Sin; Marshal of Judgement on the caster — Mortality — Mark of Sin imparts resistance to cleanse effects

Feast of Absolution — Remove curses, diseases, poisons and unholy afflictions; cannot target self — Penance and Legacy of Sin to enemies for each affliction removed — Wide area variant — Allies gain Resistant and Integrity for each condition cleansed

Sin Eater — Increased resistance to afflictions; Resistant for each affliction resisted or removed — Integrity for each — Life force, stamina and mana can exceed baseline maximums — Consume curses, diseases, poisons and unholy afflictions on allies within the aura over time

Hegemony — Increase ally resistances, reduce enemy resistances — Sin on enemies attacking allies in the aura — Wider area; incoming transcendent damage is downgraded — Aura strength need not be split when suppressing multiple auras

Inexorable Doom — Periodically applies more of existing instances; cannot be cleansed while other afflictions are in effect — Inescapable (blocks teleportation) — Persecution — Rate of additional afflictions significantly accelerated
Blade of Doom — Dagger inflicting Vulnerable — Ruination of the Spirit, Blood and Flesh — A sword inflicting Price in Blood on wielder and target — Additional damage for each Legacy of Sin

Punition — Necrotic damage for each affliction on the target — Penitence — Damage per affliction raised by raising mana cost; cooldown shortens — Area of effect variant; cooldown cannot be reduced by mana
Verdict — Transcendent damage scaling with injury — Additional instances of Penance — Sanction — Wide area ongoing effect with less immediate damage

Avatar of Doom — Summon an Avatar of Doom familiar — Orbs detonate in pairs — Orbs consumed to inflict Harbinger of Doom — Butterflies create seeking affliction clouds; can be absorbed to enhance other familiar powers
Prime Avatar: a gestalt without a soul, "a mortal anchor for transcendent power"; its power is limited to Jason's mortal power.

Numen: spiritual domains, Akashic Speech, stripping remnant magic from killed magic entities, immunity to rank suppression and to detection, tracking and assessment magic, and negation of aura abilities by fully suppressing the user's aura.

System Administrator: full access to the System, with maps, voice and image chat, party and raid features and assessment; these can be granted to a party, and Jason can open another's interface with permission or after suppressing their aura.
Relics of the King: limited access to the astral throne, astral gate and soul forge, stabilising dimensional spaces and exceeding portal limits at a cost.

Sacred Phoenix: soul abilities refined for the avatar, ghost fire added to afflictions, and on lethal damage a transformation into a ghost fire phoenix that cannot be reused for one year, reduced by absorbing life force.
Palanquin: Jason's familiars become transport; the blood familiar reinforces a form and the doom familiar adds offence and defence.
The appendix is a gold-rank snapshot; earlier screens in the series show the same abilities at lower ranks with different wording (compare for Path of Shadows).
It is "the magic core of an iron rank monster (crafting material, magic core)".
Lesser cores come from the lowest monsters; iron, bronze and higher are labelled by rank.

What a core does. Rufus: "Every core increases your abilities a little, but only a little. It takes hundreds of iron-rank cores to reach bronze rank, and that's for humans. For everyone else, it takes even more. It takes iron-rank cores when you're iron rank, bronze when you're bronze, and so forth".

What a core costs. "Every time you use a monster core to raise your abilities, it makes the other method a little less effective. The impact is minimal, at first, but every core you use eats into your potential. If you used cores to get to where I am, the top end of bronze rank, then cores would the only thing that works anymore".
Farrah describes the feel: "if you use magic cores to advance, you get to sleep in".

The magic inside a person "feels unruly, like some wild creature", and for core users it is "like feeding the beast drugged meat to make it compliant. The beast still has its strength, but the owner can't make use of it properly".

Who uses cores. "In the city we're going to, Greenstone, almost everyone uses cores. So long as you have the money to buy them you can reach bronze rank without ever facing a monster. But every rank requires more and more cores. By the time you reach silver rank, things slow right down as the costs go up significantly. Most core users don't make it to gold".
Most aristocratic families "only have a few truly powerful adventurers, while the rest use cores".

Arena fighters rank up on cores, but the professionals "stop using cores before they hit gold" because "getting to gold rank using monster cores is a tough ask"; being at the peak of silver "keeps them at the top of their game".
A grandmother taken in by a protective friend is given "money, essences and enough monster cores to rank her up to bronze".
The real method. Rufus lists three elements:
Training. Push every attribute to its limits, not just physical ones: observation, memory games and puzzles train perception, "part of your spiritual strength".
Fighting monsters. "To truly break through your limits, you must truly push up against them. Only with genuine danger can you go further and do more than you ever thought possible".

Meditation. "The other two elements are about breaking through your own limits. Meditation is about consolidating that gain. It's where you take the fleeting moments in which you were better than you've ever been before, and make that your new normal".
Aura training. Farrah adds aura training, since "your chances of getting to gold start with a good foundation, which means aura powers and aura training". See Auras.md.
Jason's assessment of a silver-rank necromancer shows "Essence ability advancement impediment (monster core taint): 94%".

Outworlders in Rimaros "carried a heavy taint of monster core use in their auras, including all of the silver-rankers", while bronze-rankers without it "showed more evidence of proper training with their aura control".

Policy rather than preference. Anna and Asya had never used cores, but "that was a matter of policy": Network executives got essences to raise them to category one, while cores were saved for frontline enforcement staff, and only committee members were raised to category two with cores.
A rare non-core option. The Network has a member who refuses cores and took eight years to reach category two.

Core users with skill. Akari, a core user, warns that "the danger is in letting them be the only source of your strength" and notes there are more core users whose skill fails their power than those who reach their potential.

The process "rendered essences unusable, replacing their powers with lesser and not entirely predictable alternatives" yet raised the implanted person "an entire rank", and the cores "commanded the absolute obedience" of those implanted.
Earth's training. The Network and the US and Chinese governments already used variants of Farrah's training programme, "for as much as a century" in the case of the latter two.

Jason's enemies in a Book 5 fight had "clearly received meticulous combat training" derived from human methods, with powers "incorporated as an addendum", which wastes the potential of a bronze-rank body.
Jason had been "trained as an essence user from the ground up", with "improved meditation techniques to get people off cores".
Jason and Farrah's programme. Introduced to the Network as a holistic method of going from "ordinary warrior to magical weapon".
Asya's frustration with being the only category one on her flight crew, because core users around her rank faster, shows the cost of training the right way.
Todd 'The Necromancer' Halverson. A silver-ranker with 94 percent taint.
Miles Cotezee. A senior administrator whose silver rank is "entirely from cores".
Cores are cheating. Akari: "There is no shame in using monster cores to grow. The danger is in letting them be the only source of your strength".
Cores are free power. They cost potential.
Training can be skipped by wealth. Rufus's point is that wealth buys bronze, not the ability to use it.
Level 2: By Book 7 the Network's outworlders in Rimaros are mostly core users in the silver rank.

Level 3: In Book 13 the Quilido Procedure is "a means of eliminating the taint of monster cores from an essence user. It was a slow and resource-intensive process, but it could unlock the potential of an essence user previously trapped at silver-rank".
Its first effective demonstration is an ex-Network paramilitary squad recruited into the Asano Clan years earlier.

In the Book 11 epilogue the national delegations Rufus meets are "core-users all" except for Rufus, the Asano scions and the US ambassador's security, who had "no taint of monster core in their auras".

Where they come from. Rufus: "Most magic manifestations are monsters. They just appear, hopefully in the wilderness, but the magic they're made of isn't stable. Eventually they break down and dissolve back into magic. Killing them just makes it faster".
The astral is "the source of all magic" and monsters are one of the forms the magic takes in a world that soaks up a lot of it.
Rank. Monsters "exist within a certain power threshold. Whether an essence user or a monster, each rank has a suppressive effect on lower ranks". They do not use essences.
Rank "was a function of their magical density, not actual power": the strongest iron-rank monsters are stronger than the weakest bronze ones, with the difference usually made up in numbers.

Lifespan and aggression. "Lesser monsters only last a week or two. They start so close to breaking down that they're aggressive from the moment they appear, but they aren't really a threat. An old woman with a broom can handle them. Iron rank monsters last about a month, getting aggressive in the final week or so. It goes up from there".

"Monsters frequently aren't a problem when they first manifest, but as they get closer to breaking down they become highly aggressive. The bulk of our job as adventurers is hunting them down before they reach that stage".
A region that has gone without hunters for two months will have iron-rank monsters in their berserk stage, while bronze monsters that spawned in that period will not have reached it.
Dissolution and loot. A dead monster "dissolved into rainbow smoke".
Anything it spilled dissolves too, and the smoke can harm a person who gets its fluids in the mouth.
The loot is whatever it leaves behind: monster cores, spirit coins, materials and the occasional essence or stone.
One blood weaver produced three essences at once, an event "less common than even a legendary essence appearing".
A monster that is not a monster but an animal does not dissolve.
Where they are strong. Magic density sets the usual rank: around Greenstone "iron-rank monsters are the norm, with a good smattering of bronze-rank. Silvers can show up, but only very occasionally".
In Vitesse's region "you get more silver rank monsters than anything. You see as many golds as you do bronze, and sometimes even diamond rank monsters".
In a saturated place monsters hunt in packs: "even normally solitary monsters appeared in packs".
A silver-rank monster can linger for years before breaking down in a low-magic area.
Diamond monsters usually come only in surges.
Intelligence. "Monsters would become more intelligent at higher ranks, their powers more exotic".
Gold-rank springclaw gorillas "were smart and spawned in large herds".
Most people know the monsters of their own area "usually by description. Most run before they ever get a good look".
Rank-up rule of thumb. "A good adventurer should be able to handle monsters one rank up, so long as the match-up is good".
Constructs and golems. Siege golems and world engineers are constructs, not spawned monsters in the ordinary sense; world engineers are "diamond-rank golems larger than most buildings".
Astral entities. Nightmare hags are "diamond-rank entities from the astral that have no physical existence in this place and cannot harm you directly".
Shape-shifters. Amalgeths "always start at silver rank, but if they reproduce enough times, they advance to gold".
Anomalies. In the transformation zones, monsters called anomalies (living, unliving, reality-dysphoric, greater) appear.
Apocalypse beasts. A creature "made from alchemy, blood and things best left unmentioned" can be a sanguine horror, an apocalypse monster that Jason says "can scour a world of life".
Monsters as familiars. A familiar is made like a deliberate monster, with a creature from the deep astral inhabiting it.

Desolation locust — no rank — A "swarm-type apocalypse beast" carried by another adventurer; Colin is the apocalypse beast in Jason's own set
Nightmare hag (second appearance) — diamond — "A diamond-rank entity that had little direct power but could manifest people's fears"
Elemental tyrant: the elemental tyrant is a silver-rank water elemental that left Jason's first and largest scar.
The fan wiki's rank pages list further monsters by rank; they are copied, tier-marked, into Wiki_Reference_Lists.md, section 4.
Monsters are evil. They are manifestations of unstable magic that dissolves; Rufus dislikes people who relish killing "everyone you find".
Rank equals strength. Rank is magical density, not power.
Animals and monsters are alike. A snake that is an animal does not dissolve like a monster.
Level 2: The haul from the Book 3 astral space is described in Book 4 as many duplicate essences from the same monsters: half plant essences, the rest mostly venom, might and animal essences.
Level 2: Jason defeats a silver-rank living anomaly of the kind a transformation zone produces.
Level 3: Blood oaks and vampires are Earth's late-series monsters; a Book 10 expedition meets gold-rank spider moles in the shaft.
Essence users and monsters share the ladder, and each rank "has a suppressive effect on lower ranks".
The ladder. Normal people with fewer than four essences are unranked. Four essences make iron rank.
Rufus names diamond as the highest rank.
The sequence in the text is iron, bronze, silver, gold, diamond.

What iron does. The System lists what iron gives Jason: damage reduction against normal-rank damage, increased resistance to normal-rank effects, aura sense, and the ability to sustain himself with concentrated magic.
Reaching iron "made your body advance closer to a state of perfection, which included purging your body of impurities".
Iron-rankers then eat spirit coins: "Then you can just eat some coins as well"; with a full set of essences a person "doesn't need to eat or drink anymore", though they can for pleasure.
Advancing past iron. A person cannot "properly progress towards bronze rank" until every essence ability is awakened.
The System then reports "Progress to bronze rank: 50% (4/4 essences complete)", counting essences whose abilities are complete.
An ability held back says "cannot advance further until all attributes have reached bronze rank". See Abilities_and_Attributes.md.

Lifespan. "All essence users age slower. At iron rank you wouldn't notice the difference, but bronze rankers can live well past a hundred. Silvers can double that; reach silver rank young enough and you'll look young for decades. Gold rankers live for centuries, and I'm not even sure diamond rankers can die of old age".
Rufus calls the idea that diamond rank is immortal "a rumour, but a persistent one" and says there is an unwritten rule that diamond rankers do not share their limits.
The same rule is part of why diamond rankers are "mysterious figures pursuing goals known only to them".

Body changes by rank. Clive says that essence users "all go through physiological changes as we increase in rank. At iron rank, our digestion starts operating very differently. Our gold-rankers here don't even need to breathe. Each time we rank up, in addition to making our bodies superior vessels for magic, there are changes to how our bodies operate".
He adds that vulnerable points in the torso are less vulnerable because the body uses them less and that silver and gold ranks are mostly containers for a living mass of magic.
Ranking up also beautifies people: bronze rank gave a woman "the healthy, athletic look of a magically idealised body".
The effect is "akin to polishing an already stunning gemstone" for people already beautiful and more striking for others.
People closer to "how we are represented in our souls" look more like that each time they rank.
Hiro and Ken regained "the healthiness of their youth" on taking essences, and bronze might "turn back the clock somewhat".
The renewal of youth is stronger with certain essences: Yumi, who chose blood, flesh and bone, looks no older than Jason.
Silver: levitation. Levitation is "an intrinsic property of a silver-rank soul, allowing the aura it projected to physically affect the environment".
Farrah calls it "inherent to silver-rank auras".
At silver rank this was "mostly just a power to levitate that helped their increasingly heavy bodies walk on weaker surfaces or even water, but it was easily disrupted".
Gold. Gold rank is where the body no longer needs to breathe, and where adventurers live for centuries.
Gold-rankers are the big names of a city; during a surge "the golds put aside their interests and agendas and step up".
The Adventure Society keeps two or three diamond-rank essence users in the largest cities "in case a diamond rank monster shows up".
Diamond-rankers are the ones who can travel between physical realities.
Mr North compares them to "a nuclear bomb that can walk around and do what it likes".
Diamond-rank monsters usually turn up only during surges, "when the hidden diamond-rankers show themselves".
Badges. Adventure Society badges are tied to the wearer's aura: "Adventurers need new badges at each rank for a reason", because a change in rank changes the aura and tracking stones stop working.

Rank suppression. "Whether an essence user or a monster, each rank has a suppressive effect on lower ranks. We're all bronze rank. If you were to fight any of us, your iron-rank abilities would have much less effect".
Resistances grow with rank disparity: a skilled iron-ranker's afflictions are shrugged off by a higher-ranked enemy.
A bandit leader assumes Jason's spells failed "due to rank disparity".
A silver-ranker fights as "silver-rank was silver-rank and the monster didn't die" even against attacks that ignore disparity.
Spirit coins offer a temporary workaround: "You can overcome that briefly by boosting your attributes with spirit coins... not for very long" and it "will leave you weaker once the strength fades".

A System text from Jason's Book 3 title says: "Ignore the enhanced resistances derived from rank disparity. This only affects the enhanced resistance from being higher rank, not other sources of resistance", and a second line ignores "the enhanced aura suppression and aura suppression resistance derived from rank disparity" without touching "the inherently superior strength of higher-rank auras".
Sophie's Boundary Breaker removes the damage reduction from disparity.
Humphrey's Hero's Drive lets him ignore resistances of disparity.
Clive notes that Humphrey and Jason "can overlook rank disparity in certain regards".

Transcendent damage. It ignores "all forms of physical and magical defence, damage reduction and resistances", so an iron-rank ability that deals it can annihilate a bronze monster. See Afflictions_Boons_and_Damage.md.
Racial difference. Cores take more for people who are not human, and humans' abilities advance faster.
The Book 12 sheet treats Jason's rank as gold with progress toward diamond; the Cosmology files cover what lies beyond.
Jason. Iron on completing four essences; his abilities reach bronze in Book 3; he says "I'm so close to silver, I can taste it" in Book 5; and he is gold by the end of Book 12.
Rufus and Farrah. Both bronze "not that far off silver" when Jason is first an essence user.
Greenstone's Society. Elspeth Arella is a silver-rank bureaucrat.
Silver-rank core user. Miles Cotezee's silver rank comes "entirely from cores".
Rank is earned only by killing. Cores let rich people reach bronze "without ever facing a monster".
Immortality is certain. Rufus: "It's a rumour, but a persistent one".
Your first rank is the same everywhere. A transformation can rank people up: becoming a corpse-host for worms "seemed to rank up the body".
Level 2: On Earth the ranks are called categories, "named after the colours of spirit coins": category one is iron, two bronze and three silver.
The grid registers incursions above category five, and "there is no above category five". See Earth_Magic.md.
Level 3: Jason at gold has progress toward diamond of 38 percent.
What it is. Farrah's summary: "Ritual magic relies on external sources of magic. That's ambient magic, plus more concentrated sources, like quintessence or spirit coins".

"External magic doesn't require you to have an essence. There are people who make careers out of learning a specialised slice of external magic", like plumbers who know "just enough to do a specific job".
The fundamental theory is shared across rituals, magical craftsmanship and alchemy: "Same basis, different applications".

The circle and the ambient magic. A ritual diagram must be adjusted to the local magic: "Every time you draw a magic diagram you need to adjust for the ambient magic conditions. A weak source of congealed magic like the core of a lesser monster is a perfect way to check your work".
A ritual room is designed with a permanent circle and a regulated environment.
A flat stone floor helps: Emir's ritual room has "a floor made from a single slab of black stone, cut perfectly level and smooth". A cloud floor is poor for circles.
Materials vary with the ritual: a salt circle will do for ordinary summoning, while exotic summons call for obsidian dust and iron filings.
A permanent brass circle is made by carving channels into stone and pouring molten metal.

Clive's gift. Clive's racial gift balances the ambient magic: "It balances out the ambient magic so you don't need to adjust your ritual circle", and his essence ability, Enact Ritual, draws diagrams in lines of golden light.
"His ability to draw them with his power, along with balancing out the ambient magic, saved immense amounts of time when going through many rituals in sequence".
Essence rituals. "Essence rituals are very gentle. It's only if you shove the essence inside yourself without one that the experience is a harsh one".
In a ritual the essences turn to glowing dust that swirls around the user; when the last essence is absorbed the dust stops glowing and falls.
The standard sequence for Sophie's stones in Emir's palace takes hours, with Clive resetting the circle between stones.
Farrah notes that "rituals that are also essence powers tend to be quick and dirty", like Gary's and her short-lived summons.
A familiar summoning is an "elaborate" ritual needed only per rank.
Large rituals. The blood cult's star seed ritual uses a magic circle "to gather and concentrate the ambient magic to fuel the star seed", supplemented periodically with spirit coins.
Carlos's soul-projection ritual, used to check for star seeds, is "a gold rank ritual", devised for the occasion and rare in Greenstone.
A circle for it was "easily the most sophisticated circle Jason had ever seen", with sections coloured red, green and blue as well as gold.
Clive's combat ritual circles glow on the floor under his feet during a fight.
Divine rituals. A god's rituals work differently: "divine rituals are not so vulnerable to vagaries of ambient magic as the mundane varieties".
They "still draw on the power of ambient magic but are infused with the glorious might of the divine. My god's will moves the magic and not the other way around".
Mirage chambers. A mirage chamber is a training room with a control block of runes at one end, carved into a stone block under a window.

It runs at a chosen rank: in Greenstone Rufus asks to borrow one but the family can only run it at bronze rank for limited periods because local magical density is low; Danielle offers hers at iron rank instead.
Formation, array, grid. Farrah is a specialist in "formation magic and arrays. Permanent and semi-permanent versions of ritual magic, which is one of the core magical fields".

Jason's account: "Formations were permanent or semi-permanent ritual effects. Arrays were formations layered in sequence or even atop one another", with "some interdisciplinary crossover with artifice".

The Grid. On Earth the grid is "like the landscape is somehow operating as a series of interconnected rituals, creating a magical array from the natural features of the world itself... nodes the size of cities, with elements made up of mountains, hills and rivers", covering the entire planet. See Earth_Magic.md.
Landscaped magic. Clive says of a large estate that whoever designed it showed "the foresight to wait for plants to grow over decades, planning out the shifts in magic as plants and trees grew".
Dice and triggers. Humphrey's summoning die activates its power by being rolled in a "simple circle of powdered chalk".
Ritual knowledge from skill books. Jason's ritual skill book gave him "the bare minimum to be considered a proper ritual magician". See Skill_Books_and_Learning.md.
Who is allowed to draw. A person who does not know external magic cannot awaken a familiar summoning power.
A ritual room with permanent circle: Landemere Vane's room, found under his burned house and described as "an ordinary, if impressive, ritual room" which "predates the settlement of Greenstone".
Portal rituals: In Landemere's old ritual room, the Builder cult's agents build an astral bridge from a brass circle and a crude brick archway.
Magic circles are universal. Each needs adjusting to local magic.
Divine rituals are just bigger. They are less vulnerable to the vagaries of ambient magic than mundane rituals.
Rituals need an essence. External magic "doesn't require you to have an essence".
Level 1: Clive's racial gift and Enact Ritual speed up circle-drawing in the Book 2 sessions.
Level 2: On Earth, Farrah is called "the foremost expert in array magic on the planet" and the Grid is shown to be a planetary array.
Ritual Magic I "can impart the fundamentals of performing magic rituals", and its only requirement is the "ability to use skill books".
Higher books list more: Astral Magic II needs bronze rank, the ability to use skill books, and basic and intermediate ritual magic theory and basic astral magic theory.
The player-style response is: "Jason was familiar with skill books from video games that instantly gave out spells or special abilities".
What happens. The book floats over the reader, opens, and its text rises from the page as glowing runes that swarm around the reader and sink into them.
The process is painful: "Using a skill book is strenuous. The more it's trying to teach you, the greater the strain".
A big book takes long and hurts more: the martial-art skill book that Jason uses was bigger than any Farrah had seen.
Staying conscious. "People often pass out while using them, but the information isn't passed on as well once they're unconscious. It takes them longer to consolidate what they've learned afterwards".
Rufus urges Jason to "try and last out the whole thing".
How it feels. The knowledge arrives as memory of something never learned: "Remembering something he never learned in the first place was an odd sensation, like déjà vu".
A reader recognises a thing as if he had always known it.

What it gives and what it does not. Rufus: "The thing you need to understand about the skill book is that it isn't going to teach you how to fight... It will teach you technique, not how to use it. It's a shortcut that saves you years of repetitive exercise, but that isn't fighting... Even the best hammer doesn't push the nails in itself".
Farrah: "Knowing isn't the same as understanding. You've used a ritual magic skill book, but knowing practical applications isn't the same as grasping the theory".

Rufus: "Learning to fight through skill books is ultimately faster than training from nothing because you save yourself years of repetition to ingrain the skills. There is a danger, however, of not fully comprehending the techniques. By preparing well before using a skill book, then consolidating well after, you avoid developing flaws in your skillset".
The Remore family academy has to beat the habit of confusing technique with fighting out of "skill book users".
Preparation. Before a martial skill book Jason is made to learn to stand, move and sit properly: "When it stops feeling awkward, you will be ready to use a skill book".

Contents are practical. "People make skill books with knowledge practical for adventurers, not for farmers. It's one of many reasons that skill books aren't proper magic instruction. They only give the flimsiest theoretical grounding".
Jason's ritual book gives him the minimum "to be considered a proper ritual magician", enough to awaken a familiar summoning power and to perform an essence ritual.

The ability to use them. Jason's racial ability Mysterious Stranger lists "Essence, awakening stone and skill-book absorption" as one of its functions, alongside language adaptation and immunity to identification and tracking.
Jason reads the description as the power to use skill books.
For others, the requirement "Ability to use skill books" is met by ordinary means, since the Remore academy uses them.
Languages. Gary notes that Jason sounds as if he "learned the language from a skill book".
Martial art. Way of the Reaper: Five Forms I is a skill book detailing "the foundational techniques for all five forms", later found in separate volumes in a hidden cache.
Jason's experience is that the forms "aren't just five mini martial arts bundled into a skill book anthology".
The skill book gave him proficiency with an array of weaponry, although Rufus concentrated training on only a few.
Opponents' view. Sophie, who has fought skill-book users, says fighting Jason "didn't feel like that".
Knowledge without ground. A reader can find a text "above his head" when the field is more specific than the skill book.
Cooking and crafts. Jason wants "a cooking magic skill book" to extricate syrup from food.
Ritual Magic I taken from Landemere Vane and read in Book 1.
Astral magic book, also from Landemere.
Way of the Reaper: Five Forms I, Rufus's gift.
Magic Society records are not skill books but are sold as tablets of public knowledge on powers.
Use it and you're good. Jason's own assumption: "Isn't the whole point of skill books to just use them and you're good?". Rufus and Farrah correct it.
A skill book is proper instruction. Clive: it is not.
A skill book makes you a fighter. It teaches technique, not the fighting.
Level 1: Jason's skill-book martial art becomes the basis of his fighting once he learns to combine the forms rather than use them separately.
Level 2: A Network enemy's training in Book 5 is derived from human methods and wastes bronze-rank potential; see Monster_Cores_and_Training.md.

Death and the grace period. Clive: "When the soul dies, it only lingers with the body for a small time. Usually minutes, but an annihilated body might have the soul depart in seconds, while freezing to death might have it linger for an hour or even longer. It's why if a gold rank healer can repair the body in that grace period, the death can be turned back".
After that, "an untethered soul is an astral object and drifts into the astral".
Outworlders. "An outworlder is someone whose soul has re-entered a physical reality, reflexively manifesting a body for itself... like a monster".
The Builder and others do not just resurrect their own minions because the great astral beings "are careful about encroaching upon one another's interests".

The Reaper and the World-Phoenix. Shade: the World-Phoenix has "the right to return mortals from death", used with restraint out of respect for the Reaper's authority, and the Reaper "only cares if you cheat being dead. Once your soul has gone to the astral, that is when it becomes his concern. Until then, it is the affair of any death god a world might have".
Jason's Nirvanic Transfiguration trades ordinary resurrection for a limited number of rebirths: "you would have only one chance to revive at each rank".
Its restriction is "not an artificially imposed restriction": a gestalt of body and soul, once it dies, stays spiritual.
The description says its restrictions "will change on reaching diamond rank".
Souls and marks. A soul "can't truly be harmed by external forces", but it can be marked.

Jason's interface "used titles to translate the scars on his soul into game terms"; in Book 3 a woman who has been watching him says she can see the scars on his soul "more clearly than the ones on your body".
A soul scar leaves a person depleted though physically well; Neil advises against rushing recovery with potions after four days asleep. See Auras.md for the titles.

Crests. A soul crest "is a magical tattoo printed not on the body, but on the soul. That imprint would appear on the body in turn, in a form that resisted design. The form of the crest was a visible reflection of the bearer's true nature".
The unique imprint on the aura stays the same even when the aura changes, making it "a guaranteed proof of identity" once recorded.
The Immortal Crest is an iron-rank consumable applied by a mystical tattooist, usable only on an iron-rank essence user.
The tattoo is purged as the wearer ranks up, so a new one is needed. Humphrey has one in vivid blue.

Healing in practice. "Most healing was done through the church of the Healer. From what he'd been told, their god supplied the essences and awakening stones that gave them their healing abilities. They could be sought out for a fee, but also sent people around the delta to heal people at more reasonable prices. It sounded good, but Jason had seen firsthand that there was always more demand for such services than supply".
Both ritual magic and alchemy have ways to heal, but "the cost and expertise required placed both out of the reach for most people".
The Healer personally tells a patient that an alchemist could not regrow a foot, and offers to station a healer at Jory's clinic.
A healer who stops a person dying within the grace period is a "gold rank healer" in Clive's account.
Messengers. Their life "is not just physical. It's tenacious": remnant life force remains after the body is annihilated and "resurrection magic doesn't work on messengers. Or anyone like them".
Diamond-rank effects. "More potent diamond-rank resurrection effects" can return the soul after it has left the body, as long as it lingers in the world, and death gods may govern them.
Recovery after soul damage. Jason's soul was "battered and beaten to the point that his entire torso was a landscape of ragged marks" and the damage gave him powerful capabilities.
Farrah's death is the example Jason's team recalls when Clive explains the grace period.
Humphrey's crest, with its blue sigil.
Jory's clinic, an alchemy lab and healing station.
A good healer can undo any death. Only within the grace period, and only against bodies that can be repaired.
A soul can be harmed. Soul scars are "marks" on a soul that "can't truly be harmed by external forces".
A crest can be chosen. It cannot be.

Level 2: By Book 9, "Resurrection magic has been harder for a few years now. Even at gold rank, you have minutes at best, and only the most complex and difficult healing magic can do it", something "the gods of healing and death did to how magic works".
Level 3: Jason's Sacred Phoenix gift lets him transform into a ghost fire phoenix on lethal damage, usable once a year.
The Interface's translation. "When recovery from soul trauma affected Jason's abilities, his interface power used titles to translate the scars on his soul into game terms".
Anyone who fully recovers from soul trauma finds themselves enhanced.

How Jason explains it. Years later he tells Delia, "It's a video game thing. Kind of like unlocking an achievement", then explains that "the soul is a blueprint for the body" and that scars on the body are a representation of defining moments.
They change the aura signature. Each window says so: "Your aura signature has changed", with a note of what can be detected in it. See Auras.md.

Godless Prophet — Jason's aura is "damaged by the direct, concerted focus of multiple transcendent-level entities" (the gods in Book 2) — Aura's suppressive force and resistance to suppression from higher-ranked auras increased; an echo of transcendent power in the aura signature —

Resolute — "The damage you suffered in your stand against a much more powerful enemy has marked your soul" — Resistance to the suppressive force of higher-ranked auras increased; his "unflinching resolve" can be detected —

Spirit Warrior — Fighting off a concerted attack on his soul by a transcendent entity — Aura's suppressive force and resistance increased; suppression resistance applies to other forms of magical suppression; after fully suppressing an aura he may attack the target's soul directly; the echo of transcendent power increases —

Indomitable — "Repeated defiance in the face of more powerful enemies and willingness to sacrifice everything for a cause" — Resistance to aura suppression further enhanced and ignores rank disparity; allies within his aura gain increased resistance —

Giant Slayer — Overcoming a much stronger enemy: the gold-rank King of the Dinosaurs — A permanent mark sensed by others; may trigger a fear reaction from the unintelligent and weak-willed if his aura is significantly stronger than theirs, regardless of his actual rank —

Reality Hegemon — A title that appears with a notice that he has "awakened potential your soul cannot sustain at its current rank" — The maximum total size of his spirit domains increases; the effect of his spirit domain on hostile intruders ignores rank disparity. A restricted effect lets him influence physical reality within his spirit domains, which he does not meet the rank to use; it is "forcibly unsealed" with a backlash for any change —

Keeper of the Cycle — Jason's compact with the Pallimustus goddess of death — He cannot resurrect himself or others; he becomes an exclusion zone for undeath energy, negating power bestowed on the undead and adding ghost fire to his afflictions —
Resolute appears again in Book 13 when Jason's System Administrator access is used to show Delia information about conditions affecting her soul, and the title window follows.
A racial gift evolution. A god or great astral being can give a follower a blessing that triggers an evolution of a racial gift.
Clive's blessing from the Celestial Book changed the human Special Attack Affinity to a spell affinity.

Harmless and irrevocable. The blessing "could not control the recipient outside of ordinary methods like gratitude and obligation" and, once granted, could be neither managed nor revoked by the giver, unlike an ability from a divine awakening stone. Clive: "The blessings are harmless".
Balanced by the great astral beings. They do not give favoured supporters blessings that contain as much magic as can be withstood, "to avoid escalation and to minimise mortal interference".
Not the same as star seeds. Astral beings can bestow blessings like gods but cannot bestow essences and stones; instead they can send followers star seeds.
Blessing powers "do not offer control over their recipients".
Given to opponents too. Some great astral beings give blessings to those who oppose their interests when ideologies mesh, or to enemies worthy of respect.

Astral blessing tokens. "Something great astral beings give out to bestow blessings, as signs of approval", usable in an awakening ritual to arrange specific abilities, which only transcendent beings can arrange.
Clive's own arrived "one night while I was studying" as a patch of moonlight.
Jason's tokens. His Reaper token, produced by his quest system, is a surprise to Clive, who says only great astral beings can produce them.

The World-Phoenix's blessing to Jason: on rebirth he is told "You have received the blessing of the World-Phoenix"; if accepted his outworlder racial ability Astral Affinity evolves to Nirvanic Transfiguration.
It is "a product of a bargain struck between great astral beings" and works outside the normal balance.
Jason had already received a transfiguration through a Reaper token, with his use of the token while absorbing a stone serving as consent.
Farrah's blessings: after the bargain between the World-Phoenix, the Reaper and the Builder, the World-Phoenix agrees if "we bestow blessings to evolve her racial gifts. All her racial gifts".

Magic Society investigators later find that every racial gift of an outworlder woman evolved through a blessing, each from a different great astral being, most commonly from the Reaper and the Celestial Book and rarely from the World-Phoenix.
The Builder "only blesses its own people".
Farrah describes feeling "all these blessings ready to evolve my new outworlder ones".
Sophie's Boundary Breaker: her celestine racial gift Astral Affinity evolves into Boundary Breaker in a fight, where Clive calls it a likely "rank-jumping power".

sec: A god's blessing on a place
claim: The Healer gives Jory's clinic his blessing and declares it a sanctuary. Compare Church_of_the_Healer.md.
The Rejector: Builder cultists call Jason "the Rejector", a living demonstration that the Builder's power is not absolute. Jason finds it "not a cool nickname".
Blessings from the Legion and the All-Devouring Eye are described as not handed out.
Humans, for example, have an aptitude for special attacks, "Human Ambition", "Special Attack Affinity" and "Essence Gift".
Elves have "Life Affinity" and celestines "Mana Integrity".
Gary notes that other races are less efficient: humans "have their essence abilities increase faster than other races". Racial gifts can evolve (see below).
The outworlder gifts. Jason's first status screen lists six racial abilities labelled Outworlder: Interface, Quest System, Inventory, Map, Astral Affinity and Mysterious Stranger.
Interface: the screens and System messages; "interpret reality through a recognisable medium".
Quest System: quests with rewards, including a "racial gift transfiguration".
Inventory: a grid of forty slots with a currency counter; items are plucked from and pushed into the screen.
Map: a self-updating map.
Astral Affinity: "Increased resistance to dimension effects and astral forces. Dimension abilities have increased effect and transcendent damage is increased".
Mysterious Stranger: "Language adaptation. Essence, awakening stone and skill-book absorption. Immunity to identification and tracking effects".
In Book 2 Jason's Interface becomes Party Interface, with a contacts list and party features that members keep while they remain in the party.
Map becomes Tactical Map, which tracks nearby allies and enemies.

His teammates' gifts evolve in the same reward: Clive's Human Ambition to Thirst For Knowledge, Neil's Life Affinity to Life Guard, Sophie's Mana Integrity to Mana Wellspring, Humphrey's Special Attack Affinity to Attack of the Mirage Dragon.
Quest System later becomes Defiant, which loses the quest effects and gains the ability to "ignore the enhanced resistances derived from rank disparity" and rank-disparity aura suppression.
Mysterious Stranger evolves into Dark Rider in Book 2.

Blessings. A great astral being can bless a person: "You have received the blessing of the World-Phoenix. If you accept the blessing, your outworlder racial ability [Astral Affinity] will evolve to [Nirvanic Transfiguration]".

Clive's explanation: such a blessing "could not control the recipient outside of ordinary methods like gratitude and obligation" and "once granted, could not be revoked like that from a divine awakening stone".
A Reaper token used while absorbing a stone counted as consent to a transfiguration.

Time magic. Time can be "sped up or slowed down" and one can "move forwards, vanishing and then reappearing at some point in the future. Affecting the past, however, is impossible. Even the Keeper of Moments, the great astral being that governs time, cannot do such a thing".
The Builder sealed dead parts of his constructed worlds in time, "frozen and unchanging", where altered things revert to the state at the moment of sealing.
Danielle's time confluence has a limited scope at silver rank.
Time and speed. Personal time-acceleration powers are very common among swift-essence users.
Rufus's sun essence "gave Rufus flashes of brilliant speed".
Immunity to identification. Jason's identification immunity means the Adventure Society badge does not track him.
Soul-based power. Spirit domains, Akashic Speech and the System itself are described in the Cosmology files; their statements are in Jason's gifts.
Removal. A divine stone's ability can be revoked; a great astral being's blessing cannot.
Humphrey's Hero's Drive. The text credits Humphrey's Hero's Drive with letting him ignore the resistances of rank disparity.
Sophie's Boundary Breaker. Eliminates the damage reduction from rank disparity.
Jason's interface appears to other people in his party.
A blessing is an obligation. Clive describes it as no stronger than gratitude.
Time travel into the past is possible. Shade: "The past is inviolate".
Level 1: The Reaper trials reward the team with racial transfigurations.
Level 2: Astral Affinity becomes Nirvanic Transfiguration in Book 4, with a limited number of rebirths.
Level 3: By Book 12, Jason's inherent gifts are the six Astral Nexus gifts and his Interface is the System Administrator gift.
Rarity is one of Common, Uncommon, Rare, Epic and Legendary; the books use the same five stages (see Awakening_Stones.md).
Essence — Rarity — Known abilities — Known users — In the book text
The wiki's table of confluence essences, each with the combinations of three essences it records and the holders it names.
Confluence — Held by — Known combinations — In the book text
The wiki's stone pages, with the rarity shown on the item screen where one is recorded and the abilities the wiki credits to each stone.
Stone — Rarity — Description — Abilities it has given — In the book text
The wiki's rank pages list these monsters.
Belinda is the team's trickster and utility caster: Magic, Trap and Adept, producing the Charlatan confluence.
She is delighted by her own power: "I was looking through the abilities it's known to give and they sound fantastic" (quoted in the character file).
Echo Spirit (charlatan) — familiar (ritual), extreme mana — Summons an Echo Spirit to serve as a familiar —
Instant Adept (adept) — special ability, very high mana, 6 hour cooldown — Large Speed boost and temporary proficiency with acrobatics, small blades and ranged weapons; more stamina —

Obsidian armour: heavy obsidian armour that glows with internal heat; a full set of glossy obsidian shards swept into wing shapes with a red glow between the segments.

Unextended it is a jagged-edge greatsword; as a whip-sword the teeth are strung on a flexible cord of red-hot lava.
Lava cannon: a showstopping power that "devoured mana like pigs with a fresh corpse"; she uses it to devastate a team of silver-rankers.
Orbs: three flaming orbs manifest over her head and shoot fiery beams; at the Network fight they are "searing flame" orbs.

Against a gold-ranked vampire, her sword hits "nothing but air" because of the speed difference.

In a duel Soramir notes he baited his opponent by burning one of his strongest abilities on a statement attack.

Civilisation-building peoples: Jason's team finds bodies of "every civilisation-building species: humans, elves and leonids, celestines, runic, smoulder and draconians" in the Book 1 desert astral space.
Where they live: the Greenstone region is human-dominated, while a port city shows "all kinds of people".
Racial gifts: "Every race has six racial gifts"; for humans they are an affinity for special attacks, faster essence advancement and latent powers that adapt to the person's essences.
A racial gift can change in "racial power evolution"; the latent human gifts are blank slates guaranteed to do so.
Triggers are often a traumatic event, a near-fatal fight or long habit; a god's blessing, or that of a great astral being, can trigger it.
Sharing gifts: the Magic Society prizes the details of racial gifts, and Humphrey advises Jason to keep his to himself and trade them for favours.

Other peoples named: merfolk ("Merfolk are not fish... They happen to be very sensual people"), goblins, fairies and valash, the last three appearing as forms taken by people changed in Earth's transformation zones.

From race to nature: in Book 12 Jason's character screen says "nature" instead of "race" and calls him a "prime avatar of an astral nexus"; Shade suggests that "race" is a term Jason took from games and cannot cover the breadth of people the System now serves.
Jason keeps the six powers that used to be racial gifts.
Older than Greenstone: "A lot older than Greenstone, with a population native to the area".
The arts: "Scholars of the arts. Painting, poetry, sculpture, dance", with people travelling from across the continent to see its theatres.
It has beautiful architecture and gardens and universities.
Look and dress: desert stone like Old City with drier air; the people are almost entirely human and very dark-skinned, with loose, breathable fashion calmer than the Ustei's.
Not a port: a coastal city that was never a port like Greenstone, with no natural harbour.
Adventuring: the Adventure Society has a branch but Boko "was not a strong adventuring city".
Boko has a mirage chamber that Clive helped rebuild.
Return of the Ustei: the Society returns Ustei captives to Boko.
Politics: its Duke is a silver-ranker through cores, as is normal for political leaders, and noble houses exist.
A movement against intellectuals among low-rankers began in Boko.
Temples: floating temples shielded by their gods survive the city's destruction.
Months and seasons: "twelve months of thirty days, divided up into early, mid and late stages of each season".
Seasons appear in the text as early autumn.
Extra days: "five additional days that didn't count as days of the month for the solstices, the equinoxes and the new year, which was at the beginning of spring".
The six-day week: Jason acknowledges "you have a six-day week".
Day names: the names are "super-simple": Jason muddles "Fifthday" and "Fourthday".

The text names no religious holiday on Pallimustus in the lines read; the holiday Jason refers to in Book 2 is an Earth one ("a religious holiday that we appropriated to stimulate the economy once a year").

Palindromic names: "in the local culture, palindromic first and last names were assigned in adulthood rather than at birth and denoted important members of a given family", most common in small families and for a prominent adventurer or high civic official; the more prominent the family, the less common the practice.
Mononyms: Zato says his name is "my only name".
Family names: "family names appeared on plaques near the entry gates" of Greenstone's houses.
The Gellers send scions from branches around the world to train in Greenstone even where they share a last name only.
Dropped names: Elizabeth the vampire says she "discarded" her last name "long before you were born".
First-name usage: using a first name is a step in a relationship; Shade uses first names only for people he likes.
Jason gives his surname and personal name in that order, "My surname is Asano and my personal name is Jason".
Given or family: people ask whether a name is "given" or "family".
Naming a being: Jason says "names are important" and that "the right name empowers us, while the wrong one has power over us"; see Lehenik.md.
Servants to nobles: "milady" and "milord".
A cult high priestess styles herself "Lady Cressida Vane"; "Lady Geller" is used for Danielle.
Officials and clergy: "Madam Director" for a director present at the star-seed ritual; "Instructor" for assessors; "Priestess Pellin". See Tone_and_Voice.md.
Royalty: the Mirror King is "Your Majesty", and kneeling is expected before him.
Messengers: "lord" whatever their sex, and "Voice Kaal" for a Voice of the Will.
Houses and titles: "Lord Headingway" is used for Ben Headingway, and "Archchancellor" for Clive.
Appearance: Sophie has chocolate skin and shining silver hair, her eyes matching it exactly, "the matching metallics a giveaway trait of the celestine race".
In Kurdansk many celestines have dark skin and silver hair.
Astral affinity: astral affinity is a celestine racial gift; celestines are similar to elves and humans.
The rare Child of the Celestial Wind appears only in races with astral affinity, on Pallimustus meaning celestines, or potentially outworlders.
Origin: Dawn says two outworlders who have a child produce a celestine, and celestines propagate with their own kind; she is herself a child of two outworlders.
Gift evolutions: Sophie's Mana Integrity becomes Mana Wellspring, her Astral Affinity becomes Boundary Breaker and her Celestial Swiftness becomes Princess of the Firmament.
Communities: Zartos is a subterranean city largely populated by celestines.
Messengers: messengers are about half again as tall as a celestine, and their servants take care never to imply the resemblance.
Dawn's true form: a celestine with ruby eyes and hair.
Greenstone's flower wine festival: a festival in the Greenstone year that Gary and his friends attend; afterwards Jason asks Bahadir "How was the wine festival?".
Memorials as celebrations: for a dead adventurer the mood "shifted from mourning to a celebration of life" at a wake.
A town festival for weeks: a small town on a lake had been "going through what was essentially a festival for the better part of three weeks" as adventurers poured through.
Wall-completion feast: a small town holds a feast with tables and spit roasts in the central square to celebrate completing its new walls.
Kurdansk parade: Neil and the others merge into "a raucous parade" in a Kurdansk street.
Rimaros after the surge: "The post-surge festivals here are world-famous".
At the end of the surge the Magic Society announces the end and Rimaros holds a lengthy festival, "a week for some much-needed celebratory catharsis".

The street festival takes over the market district, boutique ward and Adventure Society campus, with food stalls everywhere and thousands of colour-changing paper lanterns released by the Magic Society.
The aristocratic celebration ball is a political "show"; "the festivals on the streets are the real celebration".
Formalwear for the ball is tailored for the team.
See Daily_Life.md: loose breathable clothes for the heat, familiar dishes with different ingredients, spirit-coin-run household devices, heidels and the loop.

Food: the night markets of Livaros supply breakfast ingredients; the stalls serve deep-fried mash sausage on a stick (made of vegetables) and sweet-and-savoury dumplings; a woman eats a fruit pastry as Jason questions her. Jason's clifftop barbecue draws crowds.
Dress: formal pantsuits with defensive magical augmentation for the team at the ball, tailored by Alejandro Albericci, who notes leonid fashion has "given me pause".
Transport: flying carriages reach the royal sky island through a defended ring. See Rimaros.md for the city's layout.

Dress: elves wear "neat casual suits", like business suits "worn loose, with long, tapered sleeves and coattails", in light colours by night and darker shades for thugs. Elf fashion has flowing, tapered lines.
People and hair: skin tones from almond to milk chocolate, and hair from honey to rich brown, in waves, ringlets or frizz.
Food and drink: bars, cafes and places offering delights "from the chaste to the downright saucy" in the entertainment district, and small pubs with chalkboard menus.
Transport: land skimmers, carriages and personal floatation discs are present but minimal and "never driven by the elves that made up the bulk of the population".
Dress and food: the team's visit brings "new customs, new food. New sights and sounds, tastes and smells"; Jason recalls kulfi-like ice cream.
Transport: platter-sized floating discs for those who can afford them.
Dress: Jason wears tan short pants, sandals and a tropical flower-print shirt when he meets the Estercost elite.
Food: an aristocrat takes breakfast served by a butler.

Calendar: "twelve months of thirty days, divided up into early, mid and late stages of each season", five extra days for the solstices, equinoxes and the new year, which falls at the beginning of spring. The week has six days.

Clothing: "Most people, whether in Greenstone or the delta, wore loose-fitting, breathable clothes because of the heat"; adventurers on a job wear fitted outfits, often with protective properties. Elf fashion has flowing, tapered lines.
Food: preparation is often familiar, with bread, soup, sandwiches and cake, but the ingredients are mostly different because farms raise different animals and trees bear different fruit.
Jason lists local sauce ingredients with a village cook.
Housing: Leust, one of the delta's largest towns, has paved roads and stone buildings "instead of mud-brick"; in the Island, green stone appears everywhere.

Transport: heidels are "the size and shape of a horse, but with scales instead of hair and two heads, each with a horn"; the Island's districts are linked by a subterranean, submarine transit line called the loop, with terminals laid out like train stations.
Devices: lamps, showers and most household magic run on lesser spirit coins.
Communication: the Magic Society's water link projects a lifelike image of a speaker; by Book 12 Travis Noble's sky link service carries calls.

Appearance: "a member of the rare draconian race, larger even than male leonids and covered in glossy scales", the colour of dark leaves, green moving into purple; Maximilian is the tallest person in Greenstone, with a long hairless head and glossy scales.
A draconian skull is distinctive enough to identify skeletons.
Pride in descent: draconians "took pride in their claimed dragon ancestry and often had issues with other races wielding the dragon essence".

Homeland: the Dragon Lands, Pallimustus's version of Antarctica, "the native land of the large, scaled humanoids known as draconians", with active volcanoes, hot springs and "dragon mouth" geysers from subterranean apertures to a realm of fire.
Rarity: draconians are rare in Greenstone, where Maximilian is the only one present at a gathering.

The people: large, scaled humanoids who "took pride in their claimed dragon ancestry" and have issues with other races wielding the dragon essence (see Draconians.md). They are rare outside their land.
Closed society: they "aren't very welcoming to strangers" and use proxies outside their lands.
Farming and trade: the land is famously rich farmland and the best place for gold-rank cooking ingredients, because the leaking magic has earth as well as fire affinity.
Agricultural products from the Dragon Lands are the second-largest trade through Greenstone's port, after low-rank spirit coins.
Most nations tariff the goods heavily over political issues, making them a luxury food.

The land: dark stone mountains rising from green lowlands of forest and farmland laid out like a map, with a climate like Scotland or Ireland, volcanoes, hot springs and flame geysers called dragon mouths.
Name: Kurdansk lies "in the People's Holy Federation of Dreisil".
Humphrey's view: "The more they try to make a nation sound free and righteous, the more tyrannical and corrupt it is".

Denominations: "The basic coin of the realm was the lesser spirit coin. Iron spirit coins were worth a hundred lesser coins, used by bulk traders, adventurers and other members of the wealthy elite. After that, it was ten iron to the bronze, ten bronze to the silver and ten silver to the gold"; three gold coins are "worth three hundred thousand units of the basic currency".

Why the lesser coin is the basic unit: higher-rank coins are "not very useful for everyday life"; almost all home and business magic devices, such as lamps and showers, run on lesser coins and higher ranks would burn them out, while larger infrastructure such as the loop line uses more powerful coins.
Sustenance: ranked people can live on spirit coins; Rufus says a bronze coin will sustain bronze-rank adventurers without stressing their bodies, so it is about not going over your limit.
Farms: spirit coins are made on farms using special moulds that cause magic to crystallise, in delicate, very stable ambient magic.

Why Greenstone: most areas have too high a magical density to make lesser coins; the smallest denomination they can manage is usually iron or even bronze, and Greenstone was founded because the low-magic desert is a rare place for low-end farms.
A farm that makes a thousand lesser coins would make only ten iron coins or one bronze coin.

Volume: spirit coins are Greenstone's largest export, and the desert farms produce almost three percent of the lesser coins used worldwide; most farms are run by the Geller or Mercer families under Magic Society regulation.

Hazards: volatile weather, a monster spawning nearby or an adventurer using abilities can ruin a batch, so adventurers wait outside the walls; there is no defence against a monster spawning too close to a farm, and the loss is absorbed.
Control: "The Magic Society manages all of that"; coin production is the main source of its political power and the reason it must stay politically neutral.
An unregistered farm must be found and shut down.
Escorts: adventurers escort shipments of coins from a farm back to the city.
Prices: armour for an iron-rank adventurer is priced in bronze coins, which is unusual.
Wealth and rank: Jason offers three gold coins as a starting payment, and later funds Jory's alchemy facility (the amount is not stated).
Permits and trade: trade and work permits get a person into the Island's trade lanes; aristocrats, adventurers and residents use the wide lane.
Guild rewards: during a surge the contribution board adds incentive rewards above the action quota, and guilds earn the biggest rewards.
Indenture as income: criminals' indentures are sold or auctioned to recoup the cost of their crimes (see Law_and_Indenture.md).
The Sky Link Company: in Book 12 Travis Noble's sky link service is sold by negotiated special rate.
Remore Academy: "one of the most exclusive prep academies for adventurers in the world. Kings go to that school".
The family runs it, and it is "a big deal everywhere, not just Vitesse".
Rufus, a graduate, treats it as a source of method.

What it teaches: it studies adventurer methodology from across the globe so as to educate students from around the world; its students are "scions of international mercantile guilds, famous adventuring families, aristocrats and even royalty", prepared for diplomatic trouble, assassination or pitched battle.
A scouting programme gives scholarships and dormitories to people with potential.
Greenstone annex: a Remore Academy training annex with the Gellers.
It is open to all essence users, with tuition deferred until they have Adventure Society membership.

Faculty and style: the academy is "famous for recruiting adventurers, especially those close to or just having reached gold rank"; its method is "individualised outcomes", with most effort to those with drive.
Geller training: the family trains its young in Greenstone with a mirage chamber and arena; its most elite programme is entered on Danielle's introduction.
People "scramble to be on a team with a Geller who went through their Greenstone training".
In Rakesh an astral magic research wing is staffed by officials such as Lorelei Grantham; astral researchers question outworlders in a room for the purpose.
Temples of Knowledge: the Rimaros temple is an important resource for researchers, with a symbiotic link to the Magic Society and a portal chamber.
Greenstone's temple library is used by researchers.
Universities: Boko's universities draw scholars.
